title: Works, but may or may not be an improvment over similar hardware.
text:
I live within a mile of an AM/FM radio station, a cell tower, and some strong VHF repeaters. I decided to try this to see if it would increase my PiAware ADSB numbers due to greater claimed filtering depth (-80 dB). My previous setup was a FA Pro Stick Plus (blue) directly plugged into the pi with a FA cavity filter and then a short coax run to the FA antenna, which has proven to be the best setup I've tested. Without changing anything else, I replaced the FA dongle and filter with a RTL-SDR v3 (bias tee enabled) and this LNA. After a week, I compared my numbers by the same days of the week (Monday vs. Monday, etc). I average about 450k positions a day with a max range over 200 nm. With this LNA, I had consistently about 13% less positions than the previous FA hardware, and had similar max range. So it was a small, but statistically significant, decrease. The product does it's job, but I don't know if it's really going to be an improvement over a FA Pro Stick Plus+filter at the end of a coax run if that's your setup. I understand the product is meant to be placed near the antenna to provide a boost to overcome cable attenuation, so perhaps it will shine more in that role. It seems to be a good value in that regard comparted to other powered LNA options.

I am also subtracting one star for assembly quality. When I received the product, one of the screws holding the end cover on was about one turn from falling out, and the nuts on the SMA connectors were not tightened enough to fully compress the lock washer. This was easily corrected with some tightening. Soldering on the board seemed acceptable, but the edges of the board were very rough and it was placed diagonally into the enclosure because it was slightly too wide to fit in the main channel on both sides. This should not impact the functionality, but it's just a bit substandard. The SMA double male connector was also included as you see in the picture, which was convenient.

title: DEFINITELY NOT WATER-PROOF
text:
This is a cushioned, lockable, aluminum box for 10 individual 3.5 hard drives.
It is DEFINITELY NOT water-proof.
Even the pictures provided by the seller, shows there is no gasket or seal between the lid and box.
There is NO WAY this box is water-proof, as described.
However the cushioning is pretty nice, and the hard drives fit snugly into the storage pockets.
The cushion dividers between hard drives are removable, but seem to be made from poorly glued together pieces of cushion material and Masonite.
The hinges seem weak and flimsy, but may endure if not overly stressed.
The lock is only to secure the latch. It is not a security lock, and easily compromised.
The hard drive storage pockets are quite snug, perhaps overly so.
I am discovering the more hard drives I add to the box, the more difficult the hard drives are to remove from the storage pockets.
Furthermore, the more hard drives I add to the box, the harder it is to close the lid!

This box is what it is.
I don't like it; I don't hate it either.
I wouldn't buy it again

Shame on the seller for misrepresenting the product, as the box is NOT water-proof.
Profits over people!

UPDATE: on 19 April 2017, I received an email from Orico stating, "I am sorry our product haven't meet your fully satisfaction. This product can prevent rainwater from entering. I feel so sorry brought you some inconvenience."
In my opinion, this email from Orico is insulting. Not only is it insulting that they expect me to make the connection between keeping rain water out, which is barely water-resistant v/s waterproof.
Furthermore, Orico's condescending apology was more of a slap in the face, because they didn't even offer compensation for selling me a product under false pretenses. Simply - so sorry for the inconvenience that we lied! Grrr..

UPDATE: on 21 April 2017, After several back and forth emails, I was able to convince Orico their water-proof description of this box was inaccurate. Thus, they changed the description to "water-resistant." I was credited $5 as a good faith gesture by Orico.

title: Great system for the price
text: I wasn't expecting a lot from these but they sound pretty good and they are loud. I stream Spotify radio through Bluetooth and the quality is pretty good. You have to check the settings on streaming apps to get the best sound. I haven't tried the mini audio connection but I should do that. A lot of people expect top notch sound with a Bluetooth connection but as any audiophile knows, you lose a LOT of quality via Bluetooth. You are always better off using a wired connection for higher volume and better quality without pops, clicks, and hisses from radio interference. Like most people have commented, they bass is not very deep but these things will suck the life right out of your battery as is. If you added a subwoofer or deeper bass you would probably suffer performance issues on your motorcycle. I HIGHLY recommend getting a trickle battery charger for your bike and leave it on the bike while its in the garage after using this system. Your bike cannot fully recharge your battery if you use this going down the highway for more than 30 minutes and you will find it takes longer to start your bike. I gave it a try after I installed it in my garage while the motor was not running and listed to some tunes while I  tightened everything down and it completely drained my battery dead. I had to jump start it with my truck which is not really a good idea but I wanted to ride. My only real complaint is they don't provided a power switch. I bought a toggle switch at an auto parts store and installed it next to my seat. You DO NOT want to leave this connected to your battery even if you are not playing music or you will have no battery power left  at all to start it. Don't follow the instructions to hack into your igntiton either. That is not a good idea with a motorcycle or any vehicle that doesn't have a hood on it to protect it from the elements. Just a little bit of water on any exposed wires could ruin your day in a split second.

title: Great headphones with excellent sound and usability, with only slight design imperfections.
text:
Below is my evaluation after having used them regularly for about 60 days.

SUMMARY:
Before buying these headphones I did a great deal of research on the available options out there, looking at factors such as cost, comfort, performance, clarity, noise leakage, usage time between charges, and the type of power source. My primary purpose for these headphones was to watch TV in bed, without disturbing my wife. These do the job admirably and have performed very well to date, although they could get a 5 star rating from me, with a few small improvements.

USAGE:
Using these for the first time is simple, once you get them out of the nearly impenetrable and difficult to open plastic package. Simply plug in the transmitter to a regular A/C power source (or use batteries instead, if you prefer), and then plug in the 3.5mm audio cable into your TV's Audio Out slot. Then press the power button on the transmitter (it has a blinking green light once it is on). There is also volume control on the transmitter, which can increase or decrease the max volume on your headset.

The headset is easy to operate. Install two AAA batteries, one in each ear piece (see the photo showing one of the battery compartments). Then install the earpiece cushion covers, which turn slightly to lock in place. [Note: There are two AAA rechargeable batteries in the package - but you can also use regular alkaline AAA batteries instead, if you prefer.] Now just press and hold the power button on the headset until the green light on the outside of the right ear piece lights up. [Note: That little green light also alerts to you if you have a low battery, by blinking faster when the battery is running low.] The volume on your TV will NOT impact the volume on your headphones. Accordingly, you can turn your volume all the way down on your TV, if desired (the TV volume works independently of the headphones, so if the headset is being used by one person, other person(s) not wearing headphones can listen at a different volume).

Now the headset should be functioning and ready to go. If it is not operating, check to verify the following: (1) That you have the 3.5mm audio cable from the transmitter in the Audio Out slot (many TVs have an Audio In slot as well, so it can be easy to plug in to the wrong receptacle by accident). (2) That the AAA batteries are in correctly, and that the green light on the outside of the headset is blinking slowly. (3) Verify that the transmitter is on by looking for it's green flashing light. Unlike the headset, the transmitter has an auto-off feature, and may turn itself off if it is either inactive for some time.

PROS:

Sound: Excellent. No complaints whatsoever.

Volume: Good volume range, with a mute feature (it mutes if you press the volume down button after getting to the lowest volume setting). Only oddity is the volume on both the transmitter and the headset (see the CONS below for more info on this). There are separate Volume Up and Volume Down buttons on the right earpiece, one on each side of the power button (see attached photo). Unlike some older 900mhz wireless headsets, the transmitter does NOT cut out and give you loud static if there is a low volume in the TV broadcast. Instead, it transmits as much or as little sound as being broadcast on your media (like your TV's built in speaker).

Ease of Use: Good. Press and hold the power button on the headphones until the green light flashes, and do the same on the transmitter. Now ready to use. To turn off, just press and hold the power button on the headphones until the green light stops flashing. You can also turn off the transmitter manually if desired, or you can just let it turn itself off.

Clarity: Excellent. No popping or distortion at all, just as clear as a wired headset.

Range: Good. The range is perfect for a bedroom or living room setting. However, if you walk more than about 20-30 feet away, the sound may cut out temporarily (you have more range if you have direct line of sight without any obstructions, and less range if you walk into a garage or have multiple rooms between you and the transmitter). The nice thing is that unlike older 900mhz wireless headsets, you do NOT get any loud noises when you go out of range. Instead, the headset simply goes silent until you get back in range, and then resumes on its own once you are back in range.

Comfort: Very good. The headset can easily adjust on both the left and right side, for those with larger heads. The over-ear pads are soft and easily conform to your head. The only minor issue is that the standard earpiece cushion looks like thin faux leather, and can be a little bit warm and sweaty after using for an hour or two (see the CONS below for an explanation of this issue, and the easy solution).

Battery Life: Good. The batteries last about 2 weeks if you use them for a couple hours each day. Battery life is not quite as long life as with some older 900mhz units, but then again, the quality of sound in the RS160 headset is completely worth it. Battery life would likely be better if the headset used AA batteries instead of AAA, but that would also add weight, so hard to say if it would be worth it. Replacing batteries is a 30 second affair, just gently twist the earpiece cushions to pop them off, and replace both of the AAA batteries (one on each side).

CONS:

Button Function & Placement: The volume up and down buttons work fine, but even though the Volume Up button is slightly larger than the Volume Down button, it is easy to hit the wrong button by accident (especially if you don't have tiny child-size fingers). What makes this worse is that Sennheiser has put the power button in the same spot, such that you can hit the power button by accident. [Note: There is a SLIGHT imprint on the power button that you can feel if you pay attention, but it is very easy to press a volume button together or instead since the buttons are small and a little too close together.] IMHO, the headset would be far easier to use if the power button were either moved further away from the volume buttons, or if it were merely an On/Off switch.

Transmitter Auto-Off: This is the only wireless headset I have had which has a transmitter that needs to be turned on every single time you use the headset. Why does the transmitter turn itself off at all if it is plugged in? IMHO, it would be far better if Sennheiser just deleted the auto-off feature, or used a traditional On/Off power button.

Lack of any Headset Auto-Off: Unlike the transmitter, which is plugged in, it would make sense for the headset to have an auto-off feature when there is no transmission for a period of time (say, an hour). However, there is no auto-off feature on the headset. With it being difficult to know for certain if you hit the power button to turn the headset off (such as when you fall asleep with the headphones on), it is easy to accidentally leave the headset on for hours/days, running down the battery.

Transmitter Volume Adjustment: Really don't understand why there is a volume adjustment on the transmitter. If you increase the volume on the transmitter, it increases the max volume and min volume on the headset. Why not just give the headset more range of volume on its own and ditch the separate transmitter volume???

Sub-Par Material on the Ear Pads: The standard earpiece cushions look like thin faux leather. I have seen this material deteriorate over time on other similar products, and based on the other reviews I see here, apparently this occurs over time with the standard RS160 ear pads as well. However, more importantly, the earpiece cushions get a little bit warm and sweaty after using them for an hour or two. However, you can order the [[ASIN:B00884QRPM Genuine Replacement Ear pads SENNHEISER RS180 HDR180 Ear cushions Foam Earpad]] as perfect fit replacement, and get the superb velour earpiece cushions from the more expensive RS180 Sennheiser headset instead (they are a little pricey, but are worth the price).

BOTTOM LINE:

Very good product with excellent sound, clarity and comfort. Glad that I purchased them, and would do so again. While the Sennheiser RS160 has some minor drawbacks, in my opinion it is still the best option in this price range.

title: Pretty much Plug-and-Play
text:
Pretty much Plug-and-Play. After my 6 year old Dell Laptop conked out unexpectedly, I needed something fast to pay my bills, read my emails, send emails, work from home etc. etc.. I didn't have time to send the old computer for repairs, because it would probably take too long. I saw this unit selling at a local retailer for about $15 more than it was selling on Amazon. Still I didn't have time to wait for the unit to ship to my house. I Purchased the unit from the local retailer and took it home. It took me about 10 minutes to set the whole thing up and I was happily surfing the web at speeds MUCH faster than on my old computer. There were plenty of "Nanny" and "GeeWiz" Apps on this computer on initial set up, but I would not really call it Bloated. Once I learned how to bypass them, it was all good. There were no Installation Discs with complicated instructions to to deal with, just plug it into the wall and the Router and hit the ON button.

The screen is a little too bright, but you can tone it down. The resolution on the screen is not that great either. When viewing photos you can sometimes see the Jaggiez like the early 1990's monitors. Other than that, the speed is more than adequate for everyday tasks(not sure about gaming) . This computer is very light(5 lbs.) so I'm not sure how durable it is. My guess is not to bring it with you on canoe trips, horse back riding, off-road driving, fishing, hunting and things of that nature and it should be fine. For the money I am very happy with this computer.

title: Sound quality is good. They are comfortable for hours
text: Bottom line: They are low key so you can be high maintenance. This is my third pair of over-the-ear SounBots. The first pair (earlier model) I used aaprox. 5 days a week for 2 years before the charging got spotty. The second pair I left in a rental car recently (*tear), but at under $20 with Amazon Prime it was no tragedy to replace them. I had a new pair waiting at my office before I got back from my work trip. They have consistently out-performed more expensive Bluetooth headphones I have used in the $200's and under range (not comparing against the Bose QuietComfort line or that level). Sound quality is good. They are comfortable for hours. Not the best for cancelling out airplane noise, unless you like your music loud. Decent running, but you can start to feel their "weight" after a few miles. However, if you're like me running, you feel everything after a few miles. Great for the gym. You can go about 45-50 ft away from your device before they lose the Bluetooth connection. I mostly use them at work to play music paired to my phone, laptop, or desktop (without deterring my coworkers from coming in my office by having my large Bluetooth headset on that basically says, "leave me alone, thanks."). I have never attempted to use the microphone function with my phone, so I cannot speak to its quality. Pairing is easy. The side control buttons work great for volume, forward and backward play (I use Spotify almost exclusively). Charges lasts longer than any other Bluetooth headphones I have tried. Approx. 8-9 hours, and recharging to get a few more hours is pretty quick (20-25 minutes).

title: A Pleasant Surprise... A Wi-Fi IP Camera that delivers what it promises!
text:
[[ASIN:B0734SM7ZK 1080P Wireless IP Camera Dome with Reset Key 4X Zoom Adjustable Lens Wi-Fi Setting By Mobile]]

This is a difficult review to write: I don't give most products "5 stars". This camera earned that rating because of its ease of setup, quality of picture (see attached photos) and "value." Considering these three factors, this Jide Tech camera deserves some attention.

The outer box arrived with good padding to protect its contents... there was additional padding and good packaging for the camera itself.

I was anxious to test out this wireless IP camera. I am a professional installer and I have been using more-expensive "brand name" cameras for my installations.At this price, I didn't expect this camera to offer quality consistent with its brand-name. I was wrong! I think most users will be quite pleased with it

Now, for the details: Unpacking the camera, you'll find the usual items (AC adapter, User Guide and Ethernet cable, which is needed for the initial setup). I plugged in the camera and connected the Ethernet cable to my router.

Because I've installed and configured hundreds of IP cameras, typically, I don't read the included directions. This time, I decided to follow the instructions , as written, so that I could experience what an end user would experience. The user guide was pretty good. It told me to download an App from the Google Play Store (or Apple Store). I was pleasantly surprised that the App immediately detected the camera on my network (NOTE: Your smartphone/tablet MUST be connected, via WiFi, to the same network as the camera). I added the default password and it was done (NOTE: Please change the default password, after you've connected to your camera).

For me, the big test would be how much configuration would be needed to view the camera, when away from the office network. Well, that turned out to be a non-issue. The camera's P2P is enabled by default and the App simply detected the camera when the phone connected to my provider's 4G Network. From the App, I could zoom in and out and focus the camera (the auto focus worked very well, so manual focus wasn't really necessary). I waited until after dark and the IR night vision gave a very clear picture 20-25 feet away.

As a technician, I made some settings changes from my PC (typing the IP address from Internet Explorer). I haven't tested the "motion detection" and "alarm" features, but, from what I've seen, so far, I expect them to work well.

The camera's 2MP resolution should be good for most applications. Many times, I avoid the the higher resolution options, because they require too much network bandwidth and data, especially over the 4G Network. The camera supports an internal Micro SD card for recording. Most of my installations include an NVR for multiple cameras and I'm glad this one supports the ONVIF protocol.

The camera is rated at IP66 for outdoor installations. Looking at the sturdy construction, I would feel comfortable that it will survive even my Buffalo, NY weather.

Keep in mind that this is an initial review: I've had the camera running for only 36 hours. However, during that time, it has passed all of my tests. I should say that I'm pretty surprised. I've seen so many ads on Amazon that promise high quality and easy setup...This one actually delivers! I will be adding this model to my inventory for customers!

title: Great sound, very forgiving of source
text:
Great pair of headphones for when you're on the go.

A really good amount of detail and clarity, similar to M50x.
But much better bass thump.
Great vocals.

Like many warmer, thumpier headphones between $150-$500, these are very forgiving of whatever source/dac/amp you use, so I never feel the need to use a specialized dac/amp with these. It does improve with the H2, of course, but the difference is not as dramatic as it is for the m50x, Utopias, HD800, T1. The Meze 99 Classics are as forgiving as the tr80/250.

I also think the Meze 99 Classics have struck a really fun, musical balance between the different frequency ranges. Not flat by any means, but foot tapping fun.

The sound profile and forgiving nature of the sound and the lightness of the Meze 99 Classics are ideal when out and about town, but not needing noise cancellation.

The original headphones I used for "being out and about, but not needing noise cancellation" was the tr80/250. It has a nice thumpy sound, isolates okay, gets in a good amount of detail and clarity, is very forgiving of the source, but somehow lacks the toe tapping fun of the Meze 99 Classics.

The only thing I wish is that these had the fold flat capability of the m50x (the analytical headphones I reserve for audio recording). Fold flat is useful for both getting into my thin iPad bag, and also when I want the headphones around my neck and out of the way.

- Apparently, there is no manual in existence. A very elementary Quick Start Guide is included but this is also the only manual available online.

I did a bit of research and testing before settling on this BT speaker. In the end, I had narrowed down the field to the JBL Xtreme, the Marshall Kilburn, and the Princeton Audio Site 1, all of which I tested at home under the same conditions. It was pretty clear after less than 10 minutes that the JBL Extreme is without any serious competition among these three systems. The sound quality alone already sets it apart. The greatest challenge with a single, small speaker is probably to make it sound as if it wasn’t a single, small speaker. Somehow, the JBL people manage to make the speaker disappear much more than either of the other companies in the sense that voices and instruments fill the room instead of remaining trapped inside a small box. The Marshall isn’t all that far behind but can’t really keep up either. With the Xtreme, one can hear every single instrument even at low volumes, and music that explores large dynamic ranges such as Edvard Grieg’s Peer Gynt or Pink Floyd’s Wish You Were Here comes across as intended. Anything from classic to R&B, punk, funk and jazz sounds better on the Xtreme than on any of the other two units. Of course, one cannot expect the sound quality of a “real” $2000+ stereo system on a single speaker for about $230 but it is pleasantly surprising what the little tube can do. In brief, I would have decided on the Xtreme purely based on the sound quality alone but it is also convincing in other aspects. Pairing is extremely simple, all controls are self-explanatory, the built and materials seem sturdy enough to withstand any reasonable use, the battery lasts forever, and even the carrying strap is of excellent quality. Everything sounds and feels as if JBL built a high-quality product. Indeed, the unit can be carried around messenger-bag-style and still sounds great to the ear of the person carrying it. This wasn’t something I was looking for but it’s a pleasant surprise. Nobody’s perfect and JBL could improve on several aspects of the Xtreme. The bass speakers are entirely exposed at both ends of the tube, which is somewhat worrisome for a speaker that is supposed to be schlepped around the house and beyond. The Quick Start Guide that comes with the product in print is rather basic. It covers 19 languages but provides only one or two sentences per topic, leaving room for guesswork, for example, with respect to connecting two speakers for a stereo setup or where to find/activate the battery indicator. That would be OK if there was an extended manual available online but there isn’t. Instead, under “Manuals & Downloads”, the JBL website offers a spec sheet, some software, a declaration of conformity and, well, the same Quick Start Guide that makes one search their web site for a more extended manual. It’s not a dealbreaker and one can work things out with a little intuition but it would be nice to have a real manual available. Overall, though, I am completely sold on the Xtreme due to its superb sound quality, built, and ease of use. With some protective covers over the bass speakers and a real manual it would be the perfect product.

Update: I have meanwhile purchased a second JBL Xtreme and paired it with the first one to produce true stereo sound. After giving a single Xtreme a 5-star rating, I would give the pair of them a 6-star rating if I could. The sound quality is simply incredible for this price point. I am not sure if one could easily find an amplifier and two hardwired speakers producing such a sound for less than $500 total. It is amazing what comes out of this system whether using it to play music or as part of a mobile home-theatre setup. The additional benefits of high portability, zero cable mess, and a pleasant, non-intrusive design make the Xtreme pair my current sound system of choice for everyday use around the house.

title: Comcast didn't want me to have it, but it works fine.
text:
I purchased this modem for use with Comcast's Blast! service. It does it's job and provides error logs, which came in handy when dealing with Comcast.

When I signed up for service in my new apartment, I noticed that I would completely lose service for a few minutes at a time almost every day. I realized that the modem was resetting itself which took a minute. This just wouldn't do, so I gave Comcast a call and they immediately suggest that it is my modem and router. I was skeptical, so I looked at the error logs on the modem's internal webpage, and saw a bunch of T3 Timeout errors.

After a bit of research, I learned that T3 Timeout errors are typically caused by a bad signal-to-noise ratio coming into the modem. Most solutions to this were to check splitters and cabling. I suggested this to Comcast's telephone support, but they said it's more likely to be my equipment. So I had them send a technician out. The technician said my router was no good, and kept pointing to the WiFi signal (which I only used for one device) as the problem. Which didn't make any sense to me. So I settled on having him loan me a Comcast modem/router for a while to determine if it was indeed my equipment.

Lo and behold, the problem persisted even after switching to Comcast's equipment. I had another technician come out, who immediately checked the splitters and cabling in my building. He replaced and removed some old and excess splitters and left. The problem disappeared. So I switched back to using this modem and haven't had a problem since.

Moral of the story, is if Comcast says your equipment is bad, take it with a grain of salt. This modem works flawlessly when connected to proper cabling.

text:
Really, really bad image quality in any setting. Tried various SD cards from Class 4 to Class 10. Made no difference. Video records in 480, still shots record at 1920x1080 but look like they are 320 pixel stills from a 1997 webcam. Came with no driver CD. USB cord is proprietary, why? What is the point of that? Video also appears magnified like it has a small telephoto lens built into it. Sadly, this is not a good thing because when you have a camera without any viewfinder or guide (like a laser) then all you get is "try your luck" getting the subject matter into the frame. Worthless as a handheld, even worse when you attempt to even sit it on a shelf because of the case's "stylish" molding, making a level shot impossible.

This camera is utterly worthless for pretty much anything. Not sure if I would even consider it a toy since there are actual "toy" cameras for kids that take much better images for about the same price point. But all in all, this camera is worth about $5 since it's 480 res. If you are buying this for PI work or survelliance then forget it. Save your money and look elsewhere. PROs

CONs
* NOT 720p. (misleading advertising)
* Stills are NOT 12 mp as advertised.

title: Audiophiles Rejoice!!
text: After waiting a year and some change for The Core to show up, it finally did and let me tell you, well worth the wait. Sound is mind blowing, life is changed. The build quality is solid even down to the packaging. The highs, mids and lows are perfectly balanced. No distortion at all at full volume. Some songs I feel like I am there live listing to each instrument being played. Keep in mind it's garbage in garbage out, so if you have low quality tracks you will hear low quality sound. Make sure they are Hi-Fi.  The "Holographic" sound is amazing.  There are no dead spots when moving in either direction of the speaker. The setup is a breeze as well. Right out the box it comes with 50% battery and upon turning it on, it is in pairing mode ready to be synced to a device. Had my phone and the other 3 speakers set up in less then a min, which brings me to my next point. Multi-room setup is a damn breeze! No wifi or silly app needed. You press a button on the main speaker and power on the others and press another button and bam, they are all synced up playing your tunes. I live in a 3 story house and it was a bummer when I would be listing to a song on the main level and went up or downstairs and lost my tunes. No more! The Core has fixed this. It's also has a optical input to double as a sound bar. Have not got to test out the battery life yet but expect it to be an average of 8-10 hours. +/- depending on volume. Comes with a nice microfiber cloth for cleaning and a handy carrying bag for travel as well. Even has a USB port to keep your device charged.  Price is high but if you truly want to experience your music like it was recorded, on a wireless speaker you need this in your life.

title: With the Mohu Leaf I receive nearly 60 channels with excellent reception. With previous products I averaged about 20 ...
text: I have tried a number of indoor TV antennas, the one I had prior to purchasing the Mohu Leaf 30 TV Antenna was a similar product produced by RCA. I got very mediocre results with all other products. With the Mohu Leaf I receive nearly 60 channels with excellent reception. With previous products I averaged about 20 and not even all 5 of the major networks came in clear. I write this review with the hope that people researching indoor TV antennas will see this and it will help them save time and money. There are 3 key reasons I got this excellent result. I) The Mohu leaf is a good quality product, 2) The Mohu Leaf allows you to connect an RG6 coaxial cable directly to the Mohu antenna. This is really important! Many flat indoor antennas come with a RG59 cable connected permanently into the body of the antenna (the Mohu Leaf comes with one too but its detachable). After thorough research I learned that the RG59 cable doesn't deliver a strong enough digital signal to the TV. It really needs to be RG6. 3) I live on the second floor of a house about 29 mile from the major city that broadcasts for my area. I ran about 50 feet of RG6 cable from my TV to the antenna and had to place the antenna in a window facing the broadcasting city. I did this after trying to hang the antennas on an interior wall as they advertise you can. That never worked with any antenna I bought. The line of sight is more important than advertisers lead us to believe. So don't waste money getting anything you cant connect directly with an RG6 coaxial cable, get the Mohu because you can, place the Mohu up high, facing the broadcast towers (or as close as you can figure) and I bet you too can get excellent results!

title: Fantastic little stereo amplifier!  Hits way above price sound quality wise!
text: This Kinter amplifier is exactly what I was looking for, and it truly sounds amazing!  I needed a simple integrated amplifier that I could attach both my CD player and hi-res portable music player to in our laundry room (my wife and I do a lot of laundry).  I tried this amp out with 3 sets of home speakers, first a pair of floorstanding high end Magnepan MMG's, then a pair of high end Polk Audio Monitor 10's, and lastly a small pair of Micca MB42X, which is what I will have in the laundry room.  I tried the amp with the more expensive speakers (since I am a longtime audiophile) just out of curiosity, to see how good it is.  I tried all kinds of music from rock, jazz, classical, and neo-flamenco and latin guitar, and the verdict is that this is a fantastic sounding amplifier, despite the rock bottom price!  The detail and timbre of this amp is very natural, and it drives my speakers to a very good sound level with more than ample 'kick' to the bass frequencies.  It is a very quiet amp too, with no discernable noise in between songs.  That is a very good thing!  Now mind you, this Kinter amplifier does not sound as good as my McIntosh or Fisher 500C tube receiver, but it comes close in many regards!  It is a 'musical' amplifier, especially for a 'Class D Tripath' unit, and from what i've read, this is the one to get, since it has better circuitry and a real internal heat sink, as compared to the cheaper made Class D units.  In summation of my review, I have to say that this amp hits way above it's meager price-point, sound quality wise, and it put a smile on my face.  I know most people say "you get what you pay for", but this amp sounds way more expensive than it is, and is one of the best audio bargains out there today!  Especially for someone who wants to put together a super inexpensive stereo system 'on the cheap'.  For under one hundred dollars, one can now buy an amp like this one, and a pair of great sounding low priced speakers like the fantastic Dayton Audio B652 Airs (with a ribbon tweeter), and be in 'audio heaven'!  My only minor quibble is that the volume/treble/bass controls feel very cheap and a bit flimsy.  I wish Kinter would have provided aluminum knobs instead of the cheap plastic ones, but at this price point it's not an issue for most people.

title: A not so great, great camera.
text:
There are a lot of things right about the Gear 360 camera (depending on your perspective, no pun intended) But there is also MAJOR flaws with it.

Lets start with the basics. I bought this camera as we're migrating to more video focused reviews for our website, and the 360 camera that records in 4K is a great idea for a lot of reasons. I'll start with the "good".

1- The integration with your (applicable) Samsung Phone is pretty great. You can zoom in, you can change the resolution or FPS.

2- The picture quality is far superior than several other 4K cameras I tested, including the 360 Fly. I can't argue against Samsungs photo technology, they've been doing it long enough and have some of the best cameras on the market. This should be no surprise to anyone.

3- I get a lot of questions about the device, it seems to make me really popular. The base can screw off and I placed it on a custom standing monopod I created, (not a tripod because you'll be able to easily see the legs due to the angles this camera catches.)

4 - It's extremely light, as you could imagine, it's very tiny.

5 - Supports Micro SD cards, I have a 32GB I use in it, but I believe it can go all the way to 256GBs. You would never fill that up though, but we'll get to that.

6 - It comes with its own PC software, it's rudimentary, doesn't have a ton of features, but it is basically required if you want to utilize any advanced editors in the future.

7- It allows for Live Viewing, and you can zoom in and out ... most 360 cameras don't give you that option, or it's very tough to do.

Now some bad things...

1 - It overheats. That is its main issue. It's not the battery life, or that you look like a wizard if you carry it on a monopod, it's the overheating. I will be completely honest here, if I knew that the maximum amount of time I get recording 4K is about 8 minutes when I'm outdoors (with it often times lasting far below that, I've had 2 and 4 minute overheats) it can get extremely frustrating. What's worse is that I never know when it turns off!

Yes - you can stare at your phone in live view and see when it shuts off, or you can look at the camera -- basically the Red BLINKING light means it is recording... BUT if you plan on doing anything "action-y" with this camera.. for example I walked around a festival... you won't be staring at your phone or camera to ensure it's doing its job.

The camera is basically the worst employee ever.
Me "Hey are you recording?"
"Yeah, man, I'm recording I got this.. go do your thing."
Me "Okay I'm going" ------ "Hey did you record what I just did."
"OH no man, sorry it's too hot outside, I just took a nap."

2 - Editing with the cyberlink software is kind of a chore. When you import files it's supposed to automatically stitch them, but I've run into a bug more than once where it wouldn't stitch them... which can get frustrating. Usually restarting the application fixes it. I only use the software to stitch the videos, then I use Adobe Premiere to edit them. Don't waste your time with the Cyberlink software any more than you have to.

3 - Samsung support is just sad. I lost my product key for the software, contacted samsung, and did their live chat support. The live chat support agent asked me for the serial number. I gave it to them, in plain text, exactly how it shows ... "We cannot find that serial number." 5 times we tried this, but they continued to tell me they didn't have it, contact their phone support. Called their phone support, and waited on hold, after about the 5th minute, I hung up, got up.. and searched the house for the product key. I ended up finding it. Samsung is the champion of "Do it yourself", heaven forbid I actually did lose the product key, I'd have spent half the day trying to retrieve it.

Overall - at my recent event someone asked me - "Hey do you guys do weddings? Can you record my wedding with that?" And I said - NO. I wouldn't trust this camera to anyone that really expects to catch those vital, important moments in their life they want to remember. I'd have said this camera is a kind of false advertising but, they never really state a recording time. ALL pre-thousand dollar 360 4K cameras overheat. I knew this going in, but I was told I'd get 30 minutes out of it, which is better than 8.

This camera is unreliable. It's still the best camera you can get for the price (even the best camera you can get for under 800 right now). This will eventually change as the technology progresses, but for now, buy this with the knowledge that you'll have to micromanage this device.

title: Well deserved four stars!!!
text:
So I have been shopping for a security camera that is more of an event monitor for a while. Don’t live in a high crime area but want to keep an eye on the house. The Sens8 had all the features I was looking for but I never heard of them. I figured to give it a shot. I started with the Sens8 outdoor camera with light. The hardware is solid. Was easy to set up. The app is a little sluggish but it all works. The first 24 hours it took some time to upload. But after that the camera seems to acclimate to my WiFi and now runs with no issues. I then tried the first generation indoor camera from Sens8. When I first took it out of the box I was struck by its shear beauty and design. I plugged it in and it took a couple times to find the router. As it ran I noticed that it was much slower than he newer outdoor camera. The upload of a 8.5mb video file was taking hours. I called Sens8 and I was connected with a tech in California I believe. They were fantastic and sent me a replacement and in two days I got it. Again took a couple times to find WiFi. This unit was working great. Uploads were like the outdoor camera. When I listened to the live or recorded feed there was a loud crackle that make the audio no good. I emailed Sens8 and they sent me a third unit. Well the third time was a charm. All is good with a little crackle in the audio which I can live with. Since then I purchased a second outdoor camera that again works perfect being the second generation.

With all this said I am very happy with the Sens8 outdoor camera. It is a second generation product from a new company that wants to make things right with the consumer. If you are looking for an event monitor that does not have subscription fees and sends footage to an external server like Dropbox or Google Drive this is the unit for your.

If you want 24/7 security this is not the unit for your.

title: Great First Machine For Upgrading/Learning - Not A Spectacular Gaming PC Otherwise
text:
I'm very grateful for the affordability of this gaming machine, but if this is your first gaming rig, there are some things you should probably know. I wanted to post a follow up review around a year later. I've had the machine about a year-and-a-half now.

I noticed the machine was struggling with the relatively recent Cities Skylines. It was once playing Skyrim on the highest settings with extreme fluidity. I'm not quite sure what happened as everything seemed to be in working order and I did everything I could that would typically fix performance issues, but after about a year the machine really began having some issues in terms of running games. I didn't fault the machine - I knew it was inexpensive and I figured it was time to start upgrading. That was the whole point of buying this machine. I could upgrade it.

As I started upgrading, I consulted PC Gamer magazine for parts ideas. In the back they usually have a current "budget build", "mid-range build", and the "high-end" build. This machine was so far removed from the "budget build" that I was pretty shocked. Anyone with a general knowledge of PC maintenance and repair could have built the same rig for half the cost. Granted, that's without the keyboard and mouse, but if you want to game I would suggest getting a different keyboard and mouse anyways. It was nice of Cybertron to include them, but they're pretty much back-up/spare parts quality. The kind of keyboard and mouse you'd use for "facebook, email, and online shopping." They went immediately to the parts tote in my basement. Some of the internal parts were a few years out of date, even in regards to the year I purchased it. They were extremely low-budget parts even then. I'm not sure if they made any changes to the product, the meat and potatoes seems to be the same, but I checked my RAM with Speccy and it was 800 Mhz, not 1600. The power supply was only 450 watts. It's seriously the first thing I would suggest upgrading if you plan to use this machine as a starting point (something other reviewers have pointed out).

On the plus-side, it was a great starting point for an upgrade-able gaming rig. I was able to learn a lot through researching the parts and researching replacement parts. It performed about where I expected in regards to its price, but as I said, I was shocked by how cheap all the parts actually were. When I decided to upgrade, I pretty much had to upgrade everything - and I went for somewhere between a current budget machine and a mid-range machine. I kept only the DVD drive since I rarely used it anyway, and I kept the cooler and HDD, but I plan on upgrading those as soon as I can. That being said, knowing what this cheap little guy could handle, I knew my low-mid machine was going to be more than suitable for my needs.

If you're looking for a cheap machine to upgrade and learn with, this is fantastic. If you're hoping to get a nice gaming PC and don't know much about the hardware and software, you're going to want to spend quite a bit more cash on something beefier and more current.

Another plus was the lack of bloatware and unnecessary extras. I'm very comfortable just cloning the HDD to my next drive when I get to that junction.

I hope this review was helpful!

title: Put a TV on it.
text:
I'm pretty sure this will be the 5,829th review for this item, 3/4 of which are 5 stars. Why bother writing another? Cause it's actually that good. Consider all these fine points:

1) I've never installed a TV mount in my life, and had this thing on the wall in five minutes. Single stud mount. It even made me feel like a single stud after I was done. The bubble level that is included is magnetic, so you can let it rest on the mount's arm while you're finding the right spot.

2) The box weighs a ton. Why? Because, along with all the stuff you need, they just sent you 10 lbs of stuff you *might* need, in case some other company left you hanging. Maybe, like me, you wanted to mount a Vizio E32, and you wondered, why would you do this to me Vizio? Can't you just include four little mounting screws in this big ol' box? Don't worry; just look in the Cheetah box! There they are! And then, maybe you're fickle and you decide that 32" is a little small so you upgrade to the Samsung 40J6200, and you get home to realize that the mounting screws are sold separately. Of course! After taking a smoke break, check inside the Cheetah box. Whhaaaat! They're ALSO in there. Tons of extra bolts, spacers, nuts, screws, various extendable arms, HDMI cable.. don't like the paw logo in grey? That's ok because it comes with a blue one you can swap out. Point is, if it's not in here, you probably don't need it.

3) I tested this with a 43" piece of cardboard that I was pretending was a TV, and with the arm fully extended was able to rotate it to a 90° angle from the mount. Your mileage may vary slightly with a non-pretend TV, but my 40" definitely will go the full 180. The length of the arm also makes it a great mount if you want your TV centered on a wall but the nearest stud is a foot and a half away.

Seriously, it's a $25 TV mount and it's amazing. Just give it a shot.

title: Suunto Ambit3 Misses the Mark
text:
Well, I wanted nothing more than to love my birthday purchase for myself: the Suunto Ambit3 Sport. After a ton of research, and realizing there wasn't a perfect solution, I decided to go with the less expensive - but more Apple-like - Suunto. Sadly, it hasn't lived up to its hype.

Why I bought it: I'm an avid hiker (mostly backcountry) and just started trail running. After a recent injury, I had to do lots of lap swimming, so I loved that this watch was an all-around sports model. It was my first GPS watch; I really wanted to have the altimeter option to track our elevation gain on our hikes, as well as mileage in all my sports. The Suunto seemed like a cool, Apple-like GPS watch with neat features and lots of ultrarunners I know seemed to like it over the Garmin options. It was on sale here, so I took the plunge. Now I kind of regret it.

PROS: I'll start with the positive and say that not only does this watch look super cool (it's big, but not ridiculously so, on my small girl's wrists!), it's easy to read and does really well when switching between sports (I used it for street runs and lap swimming as well as backcountry stuff). It's a great city watch, in other words. I personally loved Movescount's movie option, and liked the layout and design of the Movescount app. I'm one of the few who didn't have too many issues with Movescount, but I also didn't use it too heavily.

CONS: I wanted this watch not only for trail running, but also for my weekly hikes. (Yes, someone asked why I didn't splurge for the Ambit3 Peak - but the reviews were so similar in terms of GPS signal, that I figured I'd start with the less expensive product first). Well, here's the issue: on a recent training hike up the famous Mt. Si near Seattle - a route that is incredibly popular and well-tracked - the Suunto Ambit3 Sport lost its GPS at some point and told me the entire hike was only 5.69 miles and 2700' elevation gain (it's known to be 8 miles RT and 3150' gain). Compared with my boyfriend's GPS watch by another maker, the Suunto was WAY off and clearly dropped the GPS signal at some point. Oh well, I chalked it up to a one-time event and decided to try again the next weekend: same result. This time, more like 6.1 miles RT and 2800' gain, but still way off the mark. And this time, my iPhone's free Strava app was on the entire time and told us 7.9 miles and 3100' el gain. Wow - even IT was more accurate than my watch. Not good. I also tried it this last weekend during a long run on a local urban trail; it was in the trees, yes, but the watch quickly fell behind my Strava app and eventually was a mile behind. Something's just not right here.

All in all, I'm glad I got it on sale and wouldn't buy this watch again. I've seen that Suunto is coming out with newer and better models; I'm going to wait until I see a much better option with less reviews of folks saying they lost the GPS signal in the backcountry (I should've listened!). I know there isn't a perfect solution, but when my boyfriend's Microsoft step counter and my iPhone with free Strava app are more accurate than my watch that is BUILT for this purpose - time to look for a new solution.

I'm super disappointed, as I really wanted to love this watch.

title: Tight-fitting, high quality cables and no guess work. Winner!
text:
We live in a 1950's home that only has two outlets in the bedroom. With a Samsung Tab 2 tablet, Samsung Note 10.1 2014 edition tablet, two Samsung Note 3 phablets and a Kindle Paperwhite to charge, we have a lot of wall plugs and cords at the bedside. I also have a CPAP machine and a bluetooth speaker plugged in. Sick and tired of multiple surge strips and constantly having to borrow wall chargers for use in our livingroom, I looked up alternative options on Amazon. Anker's multi-port chargers had great reviews and I've had excellent experiences with other products from this company. Since some of our cables have become finicky, I decided to get this combo pack which included 5 cables of varying lengths (three 1', one 3' and one 6' cable).

Now, understand, I don't normally get excited about electronics unless they're sexy, sleek things with screens -- I DO oggle and wax poetic about stuff like new smartphones, laptops, TV's or tablets. However, THIS accessory is as sleek and beautiful as it is functional. From the packaging on down, Anker screams quality. So impressed was I with the packaging and the slick little sliding card advertising insert, I half wish I'd done an unboxing video -- Yes, on a charger.

The charging unit itself is solid, nothing hollow, rattling around or plasticy feeling. It has a matte finish that's easy to grip and pleasing to look at. I was impressed with how well-engineered the microUSB cables were, too. The USB ends fit super-snugly into the ports with amazing precision. The cables are pliant, but don't feel cheap. Best, the plastic overmolding housing the microUSB plug is no larger than need be to immobilize the plug. If you've ever had microUSB cables with big, clunky overmolding around the plugs, you're in for a great surprise. I can't imagine a device into which these microUSB plugs won't fit, even while in the case. From what Anker says, these cables are also durable and charge faster than OEM cables. I can't vouch for this, but if the quality is any indicator, I believe it.

I plugged all the cables into the unit and tested them -- check! My Note 10.1 and Note 3 are charging up just fine. I have not seen the dreaded "Battery charges more quickly if you use original charger" or "Charger incompatible" error messages. This charger will charge devices at the maximum allowable rate without overcharging them. Unlike some other chargers I've seen and used, you don't have to pick between 1.8A, 2.4A or other designated ports. Just plug devices into those suckers willy-nilly and Anker has you covered. I know from personal experience with Anker that they also have terrific customer service. That's one of the main reasons I bought from them.

It's safe to say I love this thing. I will post an update to my review a few months hence -- remind me if I don't!

text:
As an IT professional, I had some high hopes for this router. And it does perform well in what it was designed to do. I have 16 wireless devices in my house an my previous Linksys router just couldn't handle it. For the brief time I had this router it seemed to handle the WiFi traffic well.

The problem comes in when you actually try to do more than basic configuration. Even in the newest firmware, the firewall is nearly impossible to configure effectively. Port forwarding is limited. you can use the Smart WiFi and not broadcast your SSID.

My final breaking point was the firewall. I wanted to allow some services access from the internet, configure 3 ports in the firewall and can't get any web traffic or even pings. Tested by turning off the firewall and it all worked. Then it was impossible to turn the firewall back on. So even if I had less than 15 ports (the limit) I wanted to open in the firewall; I still couldn't turn it on.

So, if you want a big red bug for your router, and don't plan on doing much more than plug it in and go, this is for you. If you actually want control over your network, you need to find something else.

UPDATE: I did a factory restore, After entering 1 port forward, I can no longer add or edit these setting. Hitting save just resets them back to the 1 record. Just going to the firewall settings and hitting save, sets it to OFF. Can not add, remove, or enable the firewall settings.

title: Good idea, works with manual modifications, but leaves much to be desired.
text:
I got this item, and it's not even the same one shown in the image. The piping is black, not chrome, and the keyboard tray is super small for any keyboard, and the arm for the chair pretty flimsy, and too small to use mounting equipment with my chair, an Aeron.

First I was going to send it back, but being a pain in doing so, I decided to try it anyways. About a year or so later, I'm glad I kept it, as it's worked wonderfully for me for most things, but would love to see a better quality version of this that wasn't built in a half-baked chinese factory.

The build quality is a bit suspect, particularly the keyboard pivot point, which was really rough to use. I took it apart and found really bad flash, ie sharp metal left that made the ball not perfectly round, and rather was gouging the plastic tray that it mounted to. Some 80 grit sandpaper to the metal to remove the bad cast flash fixed this, and now works great.

I had to drill holes and ziptie the arm to my chair, which wasn't that bad, but requires to have zip ties, a drill, and be comfortable modding things.

The worst part I fight with is the clamp assembly that mounts to the chair base itself. This is a really chintzy plastic bushing that the metal arm clamps around, and I find this tends to come loose over time. First time it fell apart on me, I added some lock washers to it, which helped. Probably nylon lock nuts are necessary, but the worst problem is the plastic bushing is breaking/wearing down over time.

My chair came apart again at the base just last week, and found the plastic now had cracked in some ways, and is only a matter of time before it disintegrates fully. Thanks for the planned obsolescence china. I'm debating taking some downtime on a weekend to pull what is left of the plastic bushing to measure and see if I can get something like a Delrin bushing made (machined) to fit this.

Any better quality solid bushing at the base mount would make this thing perfect honestly, but his plastic bushing and shoddy metal parts are it's biggest problems.

title: Surprisingly good, for it's size and price
text:
It's not even close to our $500 SRS ported 10" sub, but it's not even in the same echelon, to be honest, so it's not worth comparing. I do have an Energy ported 8" sub that I purchased about a decade ago, that it can be compared to. To ensure the Energy sub doesn't sound terrible, I have to set the Energy sub's cross-over to the minimum setting (there is no LFE for this sub, only component-level inputs). The Echo Sub, by comparison, seems to be set very well, mostly pumping out very low frequencies.

From the Echo Sub I was honestly only expecting a modest upgrade; I was expecting to want to return it right away, actually. That's not the case. Even in the same room where we have our 10" SRS sub, it emits clear, accurate low-frequencies that fill both the room it's in and the adjacent dining room and kitchen (open floor plan). Our family-room group consists of our family room sound-bar (hooked up to a 2nd-gen Echo Dot, as well as SRS 10" sub and Energy 8" sub), kitchen Echo (which is actually situated right at the border of the family-room/dining-room, on the family-room side of the partition. I was expecting so many different devices to compete and not sound harmonious (at best) or cancel each other out (at worst). The subs had to be phased to prevent cancellation, but the rest of the speakers, playing together, allow for a very nice room-to-room experience!

We listen to classical music during dinner and hear it in the dining from from all angles, which has a very nice affect. While cleaning, I don't have to turn up the family Echo Dot-to-sound-bar (and sound-bar/subs), because the other Echos (and Echo Sub) compliment the family-room speakers nicely, allowing for (again...) room-to-room transit with relatively consistent sound. The benefit to this: turning up the family room set (Echo Dot-to-sound-bar and Subs) causes some low-frequency reverberation in the kitchen and other areas of the house (e.g., the bathroom). With it at a lower volume and the Echo Sub providing the low-frequency response for the kitchen and dining room area, things sound much better.

If we're solely hanging out in the dining room or kitchen area, I don't even feel the need to turn on the family room Echo Dot (and etc.). The output from the Echo and Echo Plus in the area, supplemented by the Echo Sub, sounds great.

If you're expecting this to sound like a $500 sub, you're delusional. If you're looking to add a very nice upgrade to the low-frequency output of your Echos or Echo Plus' easily, then this is your sub.

Installation: I've got very low patience and expect things (especially from Amazon) to be top-notch, and found myself only MILDLY frustrated setting this thing up - the Echo Sub took maybe four times longer than any other Echo (we have 7 total) to setup, but it really isn't that bad. The setup of this will DEFINITELY be revised to help out those who frustrate easily or who aren't savvy enough to figure things out on their own, but most people who have even a rudimentary set of tech skills shouldn't have a problem.

Setup:

1. Mine did not go into pairing mode right away. I had to press and hold the single button on the Echo Sub for MORE THAN the instructed SIX (6) seconds for the dot to turn orange.
Note: You can't SEE the color of the LED, because it's in the center of the button and obstructed by the finger you're pressing it with...while pressing. Kinda dumb ...

2. Once the sub was in pairing mode (orange light on the sub lit), things went swimmingly, using the app.

This is the ONLY part that I had an issue with, since the included instructions were OVERLY simplistic and didn't cover it. If anyone wants a more detailed how-to, just comment below and, if someone hasn't already provided one online, I'll do so.

title: Great Monitor, Disappointed in PIP and some Games
text:
This monitor came in a dented, poorly taped box, but inside that was the real box containing the monitor. I was a little nervous based on the shipping box. Installing the monitory is a piece of cake, and doesn't require any tools unless (like me) you use a vesa mount. The supplied stand clicks into place and is very nice, but I didn't use it because I have a monitor arm.

When I turned this monitor on after plugging it into an Amazon Basics display port adapter I thought the monitor was shot. The screen kept blinking off and streaks randomly appeared on the screen. I replaced that cable with the display port cable that came with the monitor and it has worked perfectly ever since.

I want to note that my monitor came with a standard USA plug, unlike what some reviewers have reported.

Physically, the monitor is sleek and attractive. The joystick control is wonderful after spending years trying to control select/1/2 buttons on the side of my old monitors. There is one poor design choice here, the power on light is part of the joystick which is located under the monitor so if you need to verify the monitor is on you have to cup your hand under the joystick to see if it is lit.

My initial impression was how bright the screen was, I needed sunglasses to avoid retina burn. The screen is perfectly sharp, and after using it for a few days before going back to work I found the fancy monitors at work seems really fuzzy in comparison. Images are particular sharp and vibrant. 4k resolution is definitely an improvement. With this resolution comes some quirks. I had to scale windows 10 up to 150% or everything was just too small. Even after doing that, the chrome browser tabs are hard to read...not the monitors fault but Googles for not allow font changes on the tabs.

The software that came with the monitor is a complete letdown. I was looking forward to using PIP to monitor a second computer while working on the main machine, but I guess I didn't understand the propaganda because the PIP feature only puts another window in its little box. Essentially, making it just the same (or almost the same) as a corner drag in windows 10. The other features of the software weren't worthy of keeping it on my machine. Now, the PBP feature of the monitor works but merely splits the screen in half so neither side is terribly usable because of the reduced font sizes. The hope of a useful displaying of two sources fell short and is disappointing.

As for drivers, I already have an AMD graphics card and when I tried to install a downloaded windows 10 driver from LG is said successful but took all of 1 seconds to run. I assume this means my driver was current.

General work, programming, word processing is phenomenal but gaming is a disappointment.

Minecraft: Moving around caused the screen to resemble old 8mm video where there would be flashes between frames. When I don't move the display looked great, but moving gives me a headache. Switching to a lower resolution doesn't seem to fix this. I'm experimenting with optifine options but nothing has worked well yet.

Civilization 5: Moving around the map was super sluggish and I had to lower the resolution to make it playable. In the reduced resolution the screen is a little blurry.

Galactic Civilization III: Again, moving around was sluggish. In this case I was able to select low-res textures and that solve the problem with no visible differences. To date, this game handles the 4k resolution the best.

Guild Wars 2: When the character selection screen popped up I said a big WOW. The details of my characters was amazing. I couldn't wait to jump into the game. Unfortunately, the game was slower, not so much sluggish but my characters moved just slower enough to notice. The big disappointment was the building and distant images. Everything was washed out and missing details. When I reduced resolution the details reappeared, but this was a letdown for sure.

Now with all the games, I'm considering the issue to be more with my graphics card (XFX AMD Radeon HD 7750 1GB GDDR5 ) rather than the monitor. I'm certainly asking the card to handle a heck of a lot more pixels per frame.

The monitor is great, but my expectations were diminished by the useless PIP feature and game play issues. At the time of this writing, the monitor is also very expensive so you'll have to weigh the price to awesomeness yourself. If your graphics card is up to the task, I can't see where you would have any issues using this amazing monitor for gaming.

title: Put your money where your ears are!  But don't go overboard without doing your homework.
text:
A close (and rich) friend bought a new pair of HD600s and preferred the HD800 for his system. He gave the HD600 to me to test and I listened to some of my favorite music on his equipment with the HD600s and it was fantastic (to me). They were very nice but I could not get them to sound nice on my less powerful system at home. You really need good inputs for HD600 and up. So...I bought a used HD590 on eBay for $30 and that sounded much better on my equipment, but they needed repairs badly. I sent the HD590 to Sennheiser for a flat rate repair ($75) and I missed them so badly I bought the HD598 new from Amazon because of the reviews and what Sennheiser.com said about them. They seemed to be essentially the same as the HD590s I have. For $150 it was twice what I could afford really but I dipped into savings and was rewarded for my jump. Well let me just say, the HD598 sound significantly better than the HD590s. These sound even better and I'm very happy with them. I'll keep my HD590s as a back up set. The cream color and wood look is very pleasant compared to dull black or grey typical of headphones. Now I have a pair of HD590, HD598 and HD600 and honestly they all sound very different to my 45 year old ears on my equipment but the HD598s really seem to feel present in my ears. The HD590s feel like they are a little father away like the music is on a speaker that is not facing me directly, but still nice and the HD600s have much wider sound with lower background hiss from my midrange equipment but sound slightly muted and a little bass shy. They HD598s have none of these "issues" on average amplifier sound outputs like I have. And for gaming the HD590s and HD598s are superb. The HD600s don't do well in gaming since my computer and consoles are not really meant to power HD600+ type headphones. I really have to crank the volume up to get the HD600s to sound. And I am usually 1/2 volume for the HD500+. I suspect that is an impedance thing and my gear is not really putting out enough bling for the HD600s to sound nice.

In my impression once you get to HD600 and up you REALLY need good, powerful hi-fi equipment with broad band amplification to use them. The HD598 and below are less expensive and are the absolute MOST you'd want to use on an iPhone or iPod like thing. I have a 2012 iMac which has decently powerful sound amplification for a computer and I can hear a big difference between the HD600 and the HD598 and I prefer the HD598 over the HD600 by a long shot. When I get a amplifier for my stereo I'll have the HD600 to really immerse myself, but till then computer music (iTunes) and games on the HD590s and HD598s is a dream. The HD598s are also very nicely made and feel good in the hands. They look heavy because of the quality, but they are actually very light on the head. Let's hope the plastic lasts. If not, off to Sennheiser flat rate repair they go to be refurbished when needed. Headphones are like cars. To get the best out of them you need good gas and proper maintenance. Headphones that get good inputs and are taken care of will perform the same year after year when owned responsibly.

Sure there are better headsets out there for much more money but try not to fall into the "well it's expensive so it must be better" logic mindset because unless you have equipment to power expensive headphones you will be very disappointed with their sound on cheaper equipment or on portable players. It's very easy to overkill a goal by spending money without doing homework on usage. Of course ANYTHING sounds better than the earbuds Apple provides with their iPhones or iPods and these Sennheisers are much more comfortable to boot.

Basically you get what you pay for in the HD598 if you have general music devices like iPhones, iPods and Pads, computers and small stereos. Spending more on HD600s on the same equipment is foolish exercise unless you can support the headphones with equipment that has proper amplification outputs. The HD598s are good all around headphones that do it better for less than anything out there today.

Summary: HD600s cost much more and have a frequency response of 12-39000Hz with a nominal 300 ohm impedance which is pretty high. Consider that typical earbuds have an 18-30 ohm impedance and you begin to "see" why the HD600 sound quiet and muffled on low power gear. The HD600 are clear sounding headphones with very nice sound presence that feels in the room with you, BUT you need a fairly nice amplifier to push through that impedance (reduces noise and distortion). If you have average amplifiers like a really nice computer or less amps like iPhones or iPads, iPods and such, you will need to crank up the volume to get the HD600s to produce sound, BUT that sound is not better sounding just because you turned up the volume. Turning up volume doesn't increase bandwidth and range of sound out put it just make a narrow range louder (high amplitude). You are NOT getting the low frequencies (bass) and high frequencies (tweets) that good equipment pushed out. You really need good gear for that. The HD600s and better headphones are basically starving for input signal on lesser amps and they sound "bad". The HD598s on the other hand have 12-38500 Hz (basically the same as the HD600s) with only 50 ohms of impedance! That's 1/6 less resistance! So "little" amps can work with the HD598s and get fantastic sound from them (but it's a little more complicated than that). The HD600s on little amps....not so much. Actually a lot not so much. The other thing to remember is that high impedance headphones can mean that your low power amp will have to work harder to make sound and you could burn out that amp just trying to hear it. Think of it like this, imagine what 50 inch rims would look like on a Honda Civic. It would look stupid and perform even less so. Match your headphone fidelity with your equipment fidelity and you have balance and sound quality. If you see someone with HD600s on their iPod you know they like to waste money. If you see someone with earbuds on their iPod you know they haven't spent enough or they are waiting for their HD598s to ship.

Basically, HD598s are HD600s in disguise but made for less powerful amplifiers so are at a lower price and sound better on Joe-regular equipment. I also find the HD598s more comfortable than the HD600s by a smidgen. The HD600s are a little tight on the ears squishing hard after a few hours. It all depends on what amplifier you have driving the headphones. Better amps get HD600+, lesser amps get HD598 and lower.

title: Great product, but about those batteries...
text:
I have owned one of these for over three years, and I paid substantially more for it than what one can pick one up for now. As a functioning unit it is flawless. It combines a high quality Monster PowerCenter with a big capacity UPS, and it improves performance of my high end AV system and functionality, all while delivering security of those components. If you have want to avoid those long reboots with your satellite receiver after a quick power interruption, or make sure your DVR is recording in a blackout, this is your product.

The unit is massive. It weighs 63 pounds and is deep. Whatever you put it in, make sure it can support the weight, and allow an extra 2 inches for your plugs in the back.

As a product I give it five stars, and in fact may pick up another pair of them now they are on closeout. It looks great, has eleven outlets (10 in back, 1 in front) a pair of USB power outlets, and full RS232 controllability. It has worked flawlessly since purchase, and I live in a place subject to occasional quick power interruptions that can really aggravate, but with this product I am no longer bothered with them.

I give it a three based on the poor information Monster has provided regarding the battery pack. I finally found a Monster tech who explained the issue and I will tell you how to avoid it. The battery pack lasted about three years for me. The unit will continue to operate as a great power center when the battery dies, it just doesn't have a UPS. Removing the battery is not the simple matter as described in the manual, but follow my instructions at the beginning and you can avoid it.

The factory evidently decided to protect the battery pack in shipping, and they basically build the unit around the battery pack, with the four batteries enclosed in a packing tray and plastic wrap. You must remove the front cover to connect the battery pack to the unit before first use. Do this instead:
1. Remove the front cover and the battery cover plate, and then remove the top cover. Careful make sure your allen wrench and philips screwdriver are perfect fits as the screws are easily stripped. You will see the battery pack.
2. Cut through the tape, plastic wrap and top plastic tray. Don't cut the wires or batteries. You will probably have to break the plastic tray, you will not be using them again. The front lip of the bottom plastic tray needs to be removed as well.
3. You can then remove the batteries either from the top or through the front opening. There are four of them, and they are heavy and connected to each other.
4. Remove the remaining packing material form the opening. There will remain some honeycomb like plastic insulation in the cover and bottom.
5. If new replace the battery pack. If replacing the batteries, remove the wires from the old battery pack one at a time and replace them exactly as wired on the old one.
6. Going forward you can easily replace the Battery pack through the from slot.

The Batteries, as Monster does not indicate what they are or how many there are in the manual or online. They are AP-1290 F2 12V 9Ah VRLA batteries. There are four of them. Buy them from a reputable dealer like Batteries Plus, where they are certified UL and CL. Rechargeable batteries of any type are potential explosive devices, so do not risk fire by buying cheap replacement batteries from an unknown source.

title: Too much wiggle room on the A-side...
text:
Fairly basic adapters. While they offer a decently snug connection for full-height USB-A male connectors, both of the adapters I received are far too loose for half-height USB-A male connectors like on YubiKeys (tested with a YK4) and some microSD to USB adapters. There's too much room vertically so that the half-height connector pins don't make contact, and too much room horizontally so that A connectors wiggle back and forth. The C end does make a decent snap into my new MBP 2016's USB-C ports, but the A end seems too shallow so it feels like you could still push the A connector further in when you really can't.

While they're decent for full-height connectors, I really need these to work with my YubiKey 4 so I have to order a bunch of competitors' products hoping they'll work better.

UPDATE 2016-12-30:
Upgrading my original assessment of the adapters from 3 to 4 stars. After posting my original review, JEDirect contacted me immediately and offered to replace my first batch of adapters to try and address my concerns. That's great customer service and a willingness to get things right :) I tried the replacements but they are still too loose for the Yubikey4. So if you're looking for a good adapter for a Yubikey4, you're better off with a different A-to-C adapter. Other forms of the Yubikey (nano, neo, secure key) may also have problems.

That said, I've used these more and tried them with some other half-height USB-A items (a microSD reader) and full-height A connectors. Almost all have done well and fit snuggly in these adapters so I need to be fair: they are better than I originally expected. My only caution remaining is that there is a lot of space around the side edges of the connectors, so other half-height items might slip left and right while being held well vertically.

title: Nice slim cover for my Kindle Fire HDX 7
text:
I love this cover! My old cover for my Kindle Fire HDX 7 (2013) was starting to fall apart and shedding synthetic leather everywhere, so I needed a replacement big time. My kindle is almost 5 years old, so I was worried I’d have problems finding something that works for me. This cover is similar to the one I just threw out, but so far I am thrilled with this one.

It is quite thin – the HDX 7 is a lot thicker than the newer Fires, but this case fits it well and is so much thinner than my old case, which is great!

The auto on and off when you open the case works well for my HDX 7.

So far I have had no problems propping it up and keeping it propped up using the grooves on the cover. Maybe lying in bed/on soft surfaces this won’t work as well as it does on a desk, but so far so good.

The on/off and volume buttons are slightly difficult to reach, but I know exactly where they are and it is not too difficult to jam my finger in there. I have no problems plugging it in to charge when the cover is closed.

The design is cute – I usually like just plain solid colors, but needed something quick and this type of case looked like the closest to what I was looking for, so I went with the panda because I love the blue color, and can tolerate cute animals.

Overall I am very pleased with this cover. I can definitely recommend it for anyone still using a Kindle HDX 7 like me and needs a replacement cover.
