title: Out At The Pictures
text:
As others have mentioned, it comes folded so expect wrinkles to be set in. It's a sort of shiny plastic material, the likes of which I would not suggest putting an iron even on low settings on. I originally folded a towel over it and and tried to iron out the wrinkles through the towel so that the heat wouldn't damage the screen, but it did next to nothing. Hopefully the wrinkles will gradually fall out as it is suspended on the wall.

Not sure if it's the wrinkles, but the screen is slightly irregular; while hanging it, I pulled each one of the rings and make the screen taught before putting a nail into the wall and it's still...mishapen. It's okay because it's still more than large enough to accommodate the projector's picture, but the OCD in me does notice it from time to time. The border of the screen is black, but it's sort of reflective as well which can be distracting. I like the rings on the screen for mounting, but they are so big that you either need large nails or hooks to hang it. If they were smaller, standard nails could be use to have it flat against the wall. Contrary to other reviews, my screen came with a black back.

Overall much better than the makeshift place holder I had, any maybe my expectations were too high, but honestly it only seems to have made an almost negligible difference in the image quality. Before I got the screen I used a shoddy combination of an old window shade and white duct tape. This is obviously more aesthetically pleasing, and I'm glad I got it, but if you're like me and you're going from a patch job to this screen, don't expect it to make magic happen. Improved clarity and imam quality yes, but it won't change, improve or enhance the image your projector spits at it.

title: And I hate giving one for a new product like this
text:
I dunno if I've ever given a single star review before (actually, I am sure ...and I haven't ...I don't do reviews of stuff I don't like). And I hate giving one for a new product like this. Especially one with hardware that is much improved over its predecessor.

But.

WTH was WD thinking? I mean, they took one of the all-time bargains in a NAS (the My Cloud), and *this* is the result? The WD My Cloud Home is a disaster.

Essentially, WD lobotomized a sterling product. Sure, sure the new model is inarguably better HW spec'd. But jeezus: they dumbed it down to the point where it's TOTALLY unsuitable for deployment in a small businesses.

Look. It's not a NAS. It's a ...let's call it a cloud drive of some sort. Kind of. And ...if you don't have the foggiest what a NAS is ...and can barely figure out how to attach to your wireless ...and your router is a total mystery to you ...this is your cloud drive. Everyone else? - Go elsewhere. This is too stupid for you.

I'm returning the four purchased earlier this week (purchased at BB, who had a better price). If you're a techie, or you've used the previous My Cloud, fair warning: don't bother.

(Note: I'm a sys admin with 30 years in the field, providing tech solutions to small businesses. Take that how you will.)

title: Best carry-on I've ever owned... Plus it has a built-in seat!
text:
Hands down, this is the best carry-on I have known. To put this in perspective, I have been to 48 states, 7 provinces and 36 countries over the past 35 years. I love to travel: by plane, train, bus, bike and automobile. I am a quirky traveler in that I frequently fly with my Xooter kick scooter which I use for transit. I travel light and pack very efficiently. The Zuca Pro fits me.

The Zuca Pro has been a game changer for me. This is a very well designed bag.

My Zuca experience started years ago when I bought a Sport bag for my son. He was in all honors classes at Middle School but as a result he was struggling to get back and forth with his book load. I was horrified when I found his backpack weighed nearly 30 lbs! After doing some research, I discovered the Sport. It has a double set of wheels on the back which allow it to climb stairs, it has light-up wheels for safety (and fun) and it is designed for use by kids, in particular, although many others use it as well (skaters, dancers, artists, makeup artists, etc). We have used it in airports but found it had some downsides. It's a bit clunky and awkward to put over your head, and the double wheels stick out far enough to be a problem in the overhead compartments. Worse, it doesn't always fit, especially on smaller jump jets; we've had to check it due to this. But that seat option? SO WORTH IT in a busy airport or on public transit! We later bought one for my middle daughter when she went to Middle School. The Sports are great for train or bus travel, for school use, and for conventions. We use them quite frequently at conventions, especially when I need to give a presentation. They are great for hauling paperwork, electronics, lunch, water bottles, etc.

I wanted a Zuca for myself, but needed something professional looking. I travel a lot by plane, often for 3-5 days, sometimes a week. I can't take a chance with having my carry-on get checked in baggage on a tight schedule. Imagine my excitement when Zuca launched the Pro.

I have been extremely pleased with this bag. It is really well designed with a lightweight yet solid aluminum frame, hard, quiet wheels and a good quality, durable nylon fabric (which is better quality than on the Sport models). The shape is a bit unique as it is tall and narrow. The benefit to this is that it rolls right down even the narrowest of airplane aisles. The downside is that it makes the bag a smidge tippy when you are walking fast in the real world. I have found that if you pack carefully with heavier items toward the bottom (as you should with any bag), you can minimize this. You also need to be conscious to hit curbs perpendicular with the bag or it might tip. The wheels are smooth and virtually silent--even on cobblestones. And unlike the Sport, they are recessed so they fit in overheads on planes easily.

The handle has a bit of play to it, but it doesn't seem to affect performance at all, despite having been used for years now. It is nice and long--something that my family loves (hubby and son are 6'4", I'm 5'10" in barefeet). It telescopes up to provide plenty of length for long legs and powerwalking. It also slides in *completely*. It is wide enough to add stability when pulling it. I have never been uncomfortable when pulling--even for 3 miles (long story).

There are some hand grips located in various spots on the bag. These are of tremendous help when schlepping the bag onto public transit or into an overhead compartment on a plane as you have multiple spots to grab. The one negative? When the bag is "stuffed-full" packed, it can be hard to get your fingers in to comfortably use the grip on top--which is used the most. It is this grip, in particular, that is ergonomically designed to be comfortable for carrying (it's shaped and texturized)... A nice feature for those times you need to actually carry the bag.

The flat, deep pockets on the sides are great for holding magazines, a newspaper, your kindle or iPad, an umbrella, etc. I wouldn't use them for storage when I check the bag through, as there is no padding to protect anything. Since I use this almost exclusively as a carry-on, the pockets work perfectly. There is also a small pocket, handy for business cards, on both sides.

There is a built-in (covered) luggage tag on the back, located between the handle bars.

I like using the included travel cover as I have been grateful for the extra rain protection on more than one occasion. I've also checked it a few times, where I've been glad for the extra protection that it provides. However, it is awkward to put on and you can't get into the bag easily once it is. It would be great if future versions included a door zipper, like on the actual bag, for access. I'd also love to see pockets on the cover. I noticed that the new Flyer version Zuca (not this model) has zippered access in the cover (perhaps in response to this need?). And speaking of the Flyer... be aware that it might not meet the new requirements of the FAA/TSA. The Flyer also is wide, which I think might be hard getting down narrow plane aisles.

The packing system is BRILLIANT. I routinely pack for 5 days when I need to wear professional attire (suit jackets, dress shoes), but I can pack for longer if going casual or to a warm climate. Seriously, this system is fantastic. The bags are color coded by size, making it easy to find your underwear or shirts, etc. When fully packed, you can remove a bag almost like it's a file folder, then replace it easily. The pouches fit well in the case, yet still allow extra room for items like a curling iron (which I store vertically, in the very back of the bag). One negative: the zipper is only one-way. Two-way zippers would really be a performance enhancement as they would allow you to add something to a pouch without having to remove it from a fully loaded bag.

There is a small mesh, elastic-edged pocket on the inside (roof area) of the Pro. I keep a spare pair of prescription glasses in this cubby, but it could be handy for prescription medications or what have you. On the door, there are two clear and several mesh pockets. One of these can be used for wet items, such as a swimsuit, which is a super handy feature to have on a small suitcase! I stash a small tube container of Tylenol, a travel size sewing kit and lint brush, a Stain-stick, a couple of travel packets of Woolite, and my electronic chargers there. The bag is soft-sided enough that it can handle a remarkable amount of extra squishing and stuffing, considering it's compact size.

I recommend buying the matching, foldable, stuff sack from Zuca if it is available. I use this routinely. It stores easily in an outside pocket, but it's very handy for last minute purchases (lunch, reading material, travel pillow, slippers, etc). It is designed to slip onto the handle of the Pro, allowing it to sit on the top platform with some stability. Consider bringing along a short bungie cord as well, as you can attach shopping bags, poster tubes, etc. in a pinch. The flat platform is great for supporting any add-ons. I have bought the Zuca backpack and the Cool Zuca (foldable cooler bag) as upgrades. While I don't use the cooler that often, I am very glad I did buy it. Another well designed product, it can fit on top of the Zuca bags or inside. It includes a 'porthole' window on top (allowing you to reach in a remove just one can or item, and folds up when not in use. I traveled from Berkeley recently with a well stocked "pantry" of artisanal cheeses; everything transited beautifully in the cooler and there was no smell. The back pack is thoughtfully designed with places to store files, magazines, a laptop/tablet, and utensil. It also slips onto the Zuca handle when not on your back, giving it a terrific versatility. The more you can roll and not need to carry, the better in my book!

Now, you've read this far. What's the best thing about a Zuca? THE SEAT! If nothing else floats your boat about this bag, this should. I cannot tell you how many times I've been grateful for it. Waiting in a long line at the airport or for a taxi? No standing room on the train? Flight delayed... again? Are your heels killing you? Have a crabby kid? Need a table? Or a footrest? Your Zuca awaits your pleasure.

I highly recommend this bag if you can afford it and you prefer to not check bags. For me, this is a lifetime investment that I regularly use. I've worn out bags in the past and I have had bags break on me *while I was on a trip*--something I wish to never experience again. The Zuca allows me to skip the baggage claim. It gives me a bit of extra comfort when traveling. I have complete confidence in my Pro.

title: Excellent Bluetooth+Wired Computer Speakers / General Purpose Small Speakers
text:
I bought these for $40 when my old Altec Lansing computer speakers finally gave out after ~9 years (due to a faulty cord, which I could have fixed, but I wanted something bluetooth.) and I'm very happy with them. They're largeish, but the size is mostly vertical so they don't take up much space on a desk. The built-in stand makes each speaker fairly stable: if they get knocked over, it'll be to the side, but even there they are quite stable.

Bluetooth works great. I bought these because they had both a wired and bluetooth connection, and both connections work just fine. There's a headphone jack in the front of the speaker, which I haven't used and probably won't ever use.

Sound quality is excellent for this price range. Bass is surprisingly good for a system without a subwoofer. I am really impressed.

I find it odd that people are complaining that these aren't loud enough: what are you trying to use them for? It's a $40 pair of computer speakers for a desk: what do you expect? I have a huge living room and they fill the room even without turning them up fully. If I turn these up the whole way, it's loud enough that it's unpleasant to stand right next to them, and perhaps loud enough that the cops might get called. Yes, these wouldn't be suitable to host a dance party in a large hall, but they're plenty loud for what they're sold as: certainly able to go a lot louder than a lot of computer speakers in a similar price range.

I'm very happy and I recommend these highly. Time will tell if the cords in the back hold up (this is usually the first thing to go on computer speakers, in my experience) but I'm hoping the bluetooth functionality will minimize the degree to which I need to move them, and thus make them last longer.

title: Hard Drive failured in less than 2 months and toshiba has bad RMA policies.
text:
I will never purchase from toshiba again if I can help it. I purchased the X300 4TB and it initially seemed to work. However in less than 2 months it started to perform very slow, and eventually had reading and writing issues. It eventually degraded to complete failure. After much troubleshooting it turns out the hard drive has many bad sectors.

Next came the RMA process, which I am currently still struggling with. Initially after using Toshiba's surprisingly not user friendly website, I started the RMA. They told me they will sent me a replacement hard drive and that I have 10 days upon receiving it to send back the defective one or I would be billed. Sounded fair to me, and that gave me time to attempt to clone the old hard drive to maybe save some data. However the next day their tech support, someone named Joshua Chancellor, sends me a weirdly cryptic email about how they need proof of purchase, and how I have to send the defective hard drive in first because it's a retail drive. This actually took a couple email exchanges to make that clear due to some poor communication. Also. They wont send me a new hard drive, they will just send me a Visa card, and only after I send back the defective drive for inspection. Furthermore, I have to pay for and handle the shipping myself, and if I want to clone the drive then I have to buy a new one myself first. I get Joshua doesn't make these policies, though he was poor at communicating all this. Toshiba has very poor customer service and bad policies. This now will in the end cost me money to clone the hard drive and ship it when it was their fault that the product is defective. Now I have to find a way to attempt to recover my data before I ship it out. My best advise, don't buy this hard drive, and avoid toshiba since it you get a defective product it will cost you in the end. I will certainly not buy from toshiba again.

title: $2499 15" MacBook Pro Retina (2015) vs $1999 14" Razer Blade 2016
text:
I bought this to replace a 15" Macbook Pro Retina (Late 2015) with the dedicated 2GB graphics card. When I was first looking into buying this computer I was hoping for a side by side comparison between these two computers and I could never really find it. So I will provide answers to the questions that I had when I was looking into purchasing this Razer.

First here is why I was switching over from an Apple laptop. For work I need to use some software that only works in Windows, so I had to have parallels open each time I am working. It would take half of my computer's resources to function the way I needed it to. Although it worked fairly well it still got to be kind of slow running both Mac OS and Windows 10 at the same time all the time. It would make more sense to have one operating system that could do everything I need it to while using all 4 cores of my processor for it. I work in IT and didn't really need a Mac. I just wanted one. It did help me troubleshoot issues that Mac users had and Windows users. I do miss having both operating systems. When I'm home sometimes I like to game. I got into gaming and soon found out how horrible the MacBook pro was at it. I could barely play games on low settings at 1080p resolution. I would only get like 25 FPS on most games that were a few years old already.. The Razer seemed to have everything that I liked about a Mac.

1) Monitor - I love the Apple Retina display and this was one of the things I didn't want to give up The resolution of the Retina display is 2800 x 1800. I also loved the glossy look. Most Windows laptops I saw before the Razer were all matte displays that weren't that good. The Razer display matches the quality of the Apple Retina display. I really couldn't tell the difference. Same glossy feel and clear pictures and colors. The one way I am disappointed with the Razer monitor screen is the size. There is a 11/16" black gap of space between the sides of the screen and the sides of the lid. There is about an inch gap on the top and bottom of the lid away from the screen. So it looks like they could have made the screen 14.5" instead of 14" or bigger. This makes the 14" screen look even smaller. The Razer resolution is 3200 x 1800. So same height as the Retina display. Just a little wider, but on a smaller screen so things are harder to read. They should have put a 2560 x 1440 screen inside this laptop. It would be more suitable to read for its size and still be higher resolution than standard HD. If the screen reached closer to the edge of the laptop lid I would have been happy. The monitor's resolution is too high to effectively use. I use an external 4k monitor at work with this laptop. It is a 27" monitor so I get to easily use the real estate of a 4K (3840 x 2160) resolution monitor while still being able to read it. I don't understand why people try to put such high resolution screens on laptops. You can't effectively use them to their potential.

2) Keyboard - I loved the layout and feel of the MacBook Pro keyboard. I can't feel a difference with the Razer's keyboard. It is super quiet and easy to use, plus with Razer's software you can change the colors of the keyboard and even have different special effects. The only thing I didn't like about Razer's keyboard is that the backlighting only shows the function keys and not the special functions like Volume or Brightness control. in the dark I have to memorize which function keys are the sound, brightness, etc.

3) Mac OS - I love the Mac OS. It is so stable and reliable. I never had weird glitches or driver issues. It just worked. It was also very easy to navigate. I also loved how when I did need to use Windows I could use Parallels or BootCamp. It was the perfect all in one OS. This was the hardest thing for me to give up. The only reason I did was for the gaming aspect of it. I had to use BootCamp to play most of the games I had on Steam. Hopefully Apple will put in NVIDIA's new Pascall cards in next year's MacBook Pro. I would go back in a heartbeat if a Mac could handle games like this Razer can.

4) Processing Power - One thing that makes me mad about Apple is they don't update their hardware that often. Their current Mac Pro from $3000-$10,000 is no different than it was in 2013. I built a brand new PC this year for $2500 which is miles above the performance of the Mac Pro. They do update the MacBooks a little more often, but still not every year like every other laptop manufacturer does. The Razer has the latest Intel 6th generation processor. The MacBook still has one that is a couple years old. However after running benchmarks on both processors the Razer was slightly faster than the $2499 MacBook Pro. Probably not noticeable enough to worry about. I just like knowing I have the latest stuff. The new processors are more energy efficient and it is something Apple could use to improve their battery life. The 7th generation processors are just starting to release so Apple will likely skip the 6th generation and put the 7th in their MacBook Pros assuming they update them around Spring of 2017.

5) TrackPad - I also love Apples trackpad, the best I have ever used. I have used Dell, HP, and Lenovo laptops and their trackpads all suck. I never used the Force Touch option on my MacBook Pro. I just never need it. I can't find any helpful use of it, but the feel, smoothness of accuracy of the trackpad was perfect. I was happy to find the same quality of trackpad in the Razer. I miss clicking the trackpad, but you can still just tap Razer's touchpad to click or tap with 2 fingers to right click. The Razer also has two clicking buttons. I never use them though. I like just tapping the trackpad. I might even like the Razer's trackpad more because it is silent with no clicking.

6) Solid Feel - Every non Apple laptop I've used like HP, Lenovo, Dell have all had flimsy cheap plastic housings that bend. The Razer feels just like a MacBook Pro so I was super stoked about that. It looks like a powder coated MacBook Pro. There are 2 vent cutouts on the bottom of the laptop housing for the fans to pull in air. Which it definitely needs considering it outperforms the MacBook Pro in gaming by a ton. The fans can get loud, but no louder than my MacBook Pro when I tried to play games on it. The MacBook Pro got so hot right above the keyboard. This laptop doesn't feel as burning hot as the Mac did. Probably due to the vent cutouts. Also this laptop is silent when you aren't playing games. So when I am at work you can't tell that it is on.

7) Gaming - The Razer can play most modern games on 1080p resolution at about 70 FPS or higher on HIGH graphics detail levels by itself. This is miles above what any Apple laptop can do. Especially if you consider this is a $2000 laptop. We have purchased the fully maxed out MacBook Pro 15" for $3300 and it couldn't get anywhere near this performance. My Mac as I said before was the $2499 version with the 2GB dedicated (crappy) graphics card. I played Overwatch on my Mac in BootCamp on the lowest possible settings at 1080p resolution. I got about 25 FPS max and it was so blurry and choppy. The Razer played the same game at the same resolution but at much higher graphics detail levels and a nice comfortable 70 FPS. The Razer is 10 times better at games than my Mac was. Plus the Razer Core you can buy as an external graphics card dock can turn your Razer into basically a portable desktop gaming computer. I'm considering buying one in the future since gaming is the only reason I have a desktop. The Razer Core would eliminate my need for a desktop. Although desktops have much better processing speeds.

8) Warranty - Apple Care is so easy to use and bring in to the nearest Apple Store. I always purchased the 3 years warranty for Apple at an additional cost. It was always worth it. Razer only has a 1 year warranty. I haven't had to use it yet, but I can already imagine you have to ship your laptop to them for repair and it probably takes a week to get it back in your hands. And who knows if they will still find a way to charge you. There are still a lot of questions I have about there warranty. I just hope this thing lasts longer than a year. We have purchased over 20 MacBook Pros for our business and they have all been in use for years without any issues. I just hope these work the same way. Only time will tell. I wish they offered an extended warranty at an additional cost.

With the Razer I had a bluetooth issue at the beginning that would keep disconnecting my bluetooth devices. I just re-installed the bluetooth drivers and it has worked ever since just fine. That is one downside of Windows machines. You get weird glitches like that you have to work around. Never really had that with modern Apple laptops. If you don't know much about computers and just need one to do work or school with for basic web browsing or email use then get a Mac. The Mac OS is much more user friendly. You are much less likely needing technical assistance with a Mac. If you are tech savvy and are willing to work around glitches Windows 10 and/or Razer might throw your way in order save money and achieve much higher overall performance, especially in gaming, then get the Razer Blade 2016. There are things I miss about my Mac, but I don't regret getting this laptop because gaming is so fun on it.

Lastly I will express some things I really don't like about Razer which is why I am giving this rating 3 stars:

1) Razer Core - Don't get me wrong I love the idea of the Razer Core and would love to have one, but the Razer Core is way overpriced for what it does. It allows you to use the Thunderbolt 3 port on your Razer to power an external graphics card to give you nearly the same gaming performance as a desktop computer. I bought the Razer Blade directly from their website and they offered me a $100 off coupon for the Razer Core which would be nice, but it already expired after a couple weeks. I was hoping the code would last at least 2-3 months. So it is $500 for the Razer Core for me now instead of $400. What kills me is that it is about the cost of a good graphics card that I would need to buy to put in it. I will have to shell out near $1000 if I want to go that direction. I think $250-$300 would be a fair and attractive price for the Core..

2) Soon to be outdated - I just bought this laptop a couple months ago and their website is already advertising a new version of it. The new laptop will have a standard Matte laptop screen option at a lower cost of $1800 (Which I might actually prefer for gaming and work since it would be easier to read. I would also need the Razer Core to game at the full 3200 x 1800 resolution that my laptop has. The built in card can only do it at low settings. High settings on lower resolutions look better), but it includes the superior new graphics card that just released. The GTX 1060. Which from what I read the laptop version of that card is supposed to be pretty close in performance to the desktop version and will likely work with virtual reality. So I could use my Oculus Rift on a laptop! Now I am stuck with a laptop I purchased 2 months ago and a much better version is expected to release soon. My version of this laptop only released in like May this year. It isn't that old. I'm bummed that my machine is already outdated. If I were you guys I would not buy this model and wait until their next generation of laptops with the GTX 1060. I'm guessing they will be out in a month or so since they are already showing it on their website.

I have side by side pictures I will later upload for you to see the visual comparisons between the MacBook Pro and Razer Blade

title: Great Portable Speaker - Not the Best Option for Echo Dot
text:
I bought this speaker as a package with the Echo Dot (which as of today 9/25/17 is being offered again at a cheaper price even than I paid for it). The speaker is compact but has amazingly full sound for it's size. It looks really great and is a solidly built speaker. At first, I had it connected to my Dot via Bluetooth, and I loved being able to move it to different parts of my house. However, because I like the Echo products so much, I ended up getting some of the original Echoes on Prime Day, which limited the need to carry this speaker around my house. Still, this speaker is far superior to the Echo built-in speaker, so I would use it on the main level of my house exclusively.

I took this speaker with me on a family vacation, and the house we rented was full of Sonos speakers (mostly Play:3s), and my mother-in-law commented that the Bose actually sounded more full than the Sonos, despite the fact that it was competing with about three of those speakers. While I can't quite agree with her, I can say that the sound coming from the Bose speaker wasn't far behind, and I found myself using it more than the Sonos, since using my own phone with Bluetooth to play my music was a lot easier than trying to find music through the iPad that had the Sonos app on it. (If the sound difference had been greater, I would have spent more time using the Sonos).

In the end, however, I decided that having a portable (battery powered) speaker wasn't the right way to go with the Dot for me. Because I own a few Echo speakers and once multi-room music was introduced (which disconnects from a portable bluetooth speaker anyway), the Bose made less and less sense. While this speaker does have a 3.5 mm line-in port (which is the only way to use external speakers with multi-room music), it didn't make sense to keep using a battery-powered speaker if I wasn't going to move it around. I ended up getting this Klipsch system, which is a bit cheaper and does sound quite a bit better, too: [[ASIN:B000062VUO Klipsch ProMedia 2.1 THX Certified Computer Speaker System (Black)]]. Granted, the Klipsch takes up a lot more space and has a lot of wires, which worked fine with where I wanted it set up in my house.

I still use the Bose Soundlink Mini II when I'm working in my basement and occasionally I'll take it to my office (where I don't have any Echo products) using the Bluetooth connection with my iPhone. I still think it's a great speaker with great sound, and I appreciate it more now again that I'm using it as a portable speaker. I definitely plan on taking it with me anytime my family goes on vacation as well.

title: These will break on you within a matter of months, perhaps weeks...Klipsch does not honor warranties!!
text:
As indicated by many other reviewers, the headphone jack wears out extremely quickly. I have had three pairs of these headphones break in the past 2 years. The most recent pair I purchased was in October of 2014 and ended up losing sound in one earbud just this past week (February 2015).

Which brings me to some issues with Klipsch as a brand. The first pair that I purchased had worn out within a matter of months. Upon placing a warranty claim with Klipsch they quickly responded by sending me a new pair (greatly appreciated), which lasted a few more months. Once the replacement pair had gone bad, I went ahead and purchased my latest pair (from October 2014) assuming that I would be covered under the same warranty. I placed a warranty claim with them yesterday, after sound goes out in the left earbud, only to learn that Klipsch refuses to cover warranty issues on items purchased by third parties on Amazon.

Their refusal is likely coming as a result of an overwhelming number of claims being placed on their poorly produced product. Sidestepping their warranty responsibilities seem to be an effort to reduce profit-loss as a result replacement and repair.

On the other hand, I decided to contact Amazon and they were quick to let me know that I will be able to receive a refund, even though I am past the 30 day refund period. I have nothing but great things to say about Amazon and their service (for this and many other instances of product displeasure), and it seems a bit of a shame that Klipsch is going to be benefiting from this.

I would recommend staying away from these and other Klipsch products. Companies that don't honor their warranty services should be avoided.

title: Great monitor mount adding a floating monitor look to any set up
text:
I have been on the look out for a dual monitor mount for a long time, going to store and seeing the outrageous prices I found this little gem. It is a great dual monitor mount, I received it in a box much smaller than I received it in a box much smaller than expected and I also didn't expect it to come in so many parts. It will take a little technical know how to assemble this Item easily, The instructions can use some work such as a written description of the screws needed in each step, I figured it out but not with out making a few mistakes. I also wished that the top portion of the base and the the clapping feet where larger. I have 2 different monitor one heavier than the other I found the mount leaning ever so slightly, and I found the mount dented my MDF desk top.
On the other side the mount is very stable, with full independent adjust ability on both monitors you can place your monitors any where with the added feature of a more professional look and available desktop space. I have used many monitor mounts and this one is one of the more stable ones out there with very little to no wobble, it really only moves when I shake the desk. Other monitor mounts have short comings like wobble, lack of adjust ability, and ease of use. If you don't know exactly how you want your monitors sit or are not sure how your monitors will sit on a mount i would highly recommend getting this mount. you will be able to adjust height, angle and rotation to your hearts content. I personally use this mount in a vertical and horizontal setup for streaming, gaming, writing, and content creation. I move my monitors constantly and I love the fact I and put the monitor closer to the desk so I can see the monitor and my hands at the same time, or move them away for when I need more desk space for paperwork of crafts, you can point them up and raise them just in case you feel like standing. The best aprt is the minimalistic look it adds to your desk and the way it blends everything together. If you are like my with mismatched monitors this will help make everything seem like it was meant to work together.

title: Traveling to Europe with pump
text:
This adapter does work in Europe. All it needs is the plug adapter for European outlets. However, with this adapter, my Pump In Style (9 VDC max) does not work at full power. Turned up to the max, the pump only has what feels like 60-70% power. This maybe what they mean by 'energy efficient' If you have a easy let down, this should not be a problem, but if you need your pump to be at full power just to get milk out then this is not for you.
Using this adapter increased my pump time from my usual 10-12 minutes to about 20 minutes with me having to squeeze my boobs to get the last of the milk out.
I was planning on keeping this as a back up, but I will be returning. The battery pack adapter give just about as much power as this adapter so I'll just be using that one in the future if I need to travel.
As well, had a hilarious time going through security at Charles de Gaulle with the pump. I've heard Parisians and French women in general do not breast feed as much or as long as Americans and this is true. They tested this pump for explosive residue and the poor agent was so embarrassed when he realized what it was haha! And just as a tip; you will NOT be allowed to bring your breast milk on the plane with you, BUT if you bring some gel packs and freeze the milk, put it in a small cooler with the frozen gel packs and put it in your suitcase, it will most likely still be frozen by the time you get home because the plane cargo holds are so cold.

title: good single 4tb 2.5" hdd but not 4K logical
text:
for those looking for a low-powered high capacity portable hdd with 4k logical sector, you will be disappointed. the single hdd in the enclosure even though stated as AF, advanced format, translates 4k physical sector into 512b logical. what this means is without an interface to retranslate back to 4k sector, you will never be able to have full compatibility with legacy device which has a limit of 32bit addressing. you will never be able to address the full capacity in MBR. you cannot format it as MBR Fat32 partition, only GPT Fat32 or NTFS or other partitioning system. you will fall back to a 2tb "max" hdd.

the only solution now is to disassemble the unit, get a 4k interface which could translate 512b back to 4k logical sector and interface with the hdd. seagate freeagent goflex interface seems to be the only option as far as i know.

title: Disappointing Customer Service.  I've included a workaround for broken Bluetooth Pairing Feature.
text:
After experiencing a problem with these headphones, I contacted Bose Customer service. While I like the product overall, the customer service that one gets for what I consider a major purchase is left wanting. After my contact with Customer Support, I was asked to complete a survey (not that it could actually be submitted - see below). The information I put into their comments section should answer any questions:

---------------------------------

1. Representatives should first listen to what has been attempted by the caller. I understand that there is likely a guide/flowchart for resolution, but having to explain to the representative "Nope, I can't do that due to the issue I've been attempting to explain" is frustrating (Rep: "Slide the switch towards the bluetooth symbol for 10 seconds". Me: "I've told you that doesn't work, but I'm doing it." Rep: "Now you should be hearing the confirmation." Me: "Nope." Rep: "Just slide the switch to the bluetooth setting for 10 seconds." Me: "I am and I have." Rep: "You should be hearing the confirmation." Me: "Nope. Because it's not working. That's why I called." Rep: "Are you sliding the correct switch <explains switch location>?" Me: "Yes." Rep: "Are you holding it for 10 seconds?" Me: "Yes." Rep: "It sounds like there may be a problem with the switch on the headphones. Please hold while I attempt to find a way to resolve this problem."

2. Representatives/Bose Support should not utilize and even use as a troubleshooting referral/tool the Community Support area on the Bose website if they are going to discredit the information given in that site. When I indicated that the bluetooth switch not working on some models of the QC 35, citing the Bose website, I was told "No, that issue does not exist for these headphones." If one reads the community support that Bose encourages users to utilize it is clear that this is a problem. If Bose Support does not think the information on the Community Support site is valid, then don't refer customers to it.

3. After paying over $350 for a luxury product, I think it was inappropriate to then ask for me, the customer who was supplied with a defective item, to then be required to give my credit card information and pay for shipping. When this happened, I actually double checked that I had contacted the correct Bose support phone number as I thought I had perhaps stumbled into a scam.

4. I was told by the representative the amount that I would be charged for shipping. When the first email was received, I was actually charged more. So not only was I required to give my credit card number, and get charged for shipping a defective product, I was not even given the correct charge. Did I stumble into a scam after all?

5. The support emails that were sent had dead image links (making it look even more like a scam) and were in two parts. The information about the "Return #" was not mentioned during the call and was not mentioned in the first email until the very end. That information should have been clear and at the beginning of the email. The second email, the one that actually had the shipping label, did not mention at all that a Return number was needed. It simply had instructions for attaching the shipping label. In short, don't split shipping instructions across two emails, make sure that relevant information is presented first, and fix your image links.

6. The emails that were sent have also indicated that I am required to now insure the headphones being returned for their $350 value. This is yet another charge to insure a product that no longer even works properly. Your returns policy is not fair and is misleading.

7. The survey asks if I would refer family or friends and simply gives a 1-10 Likert scale for likely/unlikely. I want to make clear that, based upon this experience, I will actively discourage others from buying a Bose product until the problems outlined above have been addressed. I also intend to publish this information at the site where the purchase was made.

------------------------------------

To add insult to injury, after taking the time to complete the survey, the Bose website experienced a "Runtime" error due to a configuration problem that actually presents a security risk (the customErrors tag does not appear to have been turned off, and configuration information is presented - a "no no"). Attempts to try and resubmit simply result in the same error. Their survey tool is broken.

To be clear, the Bose Community Support site has multiple posts seeming to indicate that the latest Firmware update breaks the functionality of the bluetooth pairing feature. One can still use the Bose Connection app to delete devices and connect, but 1) only on IOS and Android devices (not Windows, Linux, etc.) 2) can only connect to one device at a time, deleting the previously paired device and adding the new one [the headphones are advertised as being able to connect to more than one device], and 3) the bluetooth pairing feature on the headphones themselves remains broken.

I will be attempting to return the headphones today. Customer support indicated that after the headphones are received, it can take 10 days to verify the receipt, several more days to process, and then another week or two for shipping the replacement. Approximately 3-6 weeks from the sound of it. I carefully took pictures to show how I shipped the item back, including the RMA on 3 surfaces of the outside of the box as well as another copy inside the plastic bag that contain the headphones. And, of course, the shipping label for which I had to pay. I'll try to update how long it takes and if any further difficulties are experienced.

title: A product advertised as water proof, but is *far* from it.
text:
Though listed as "Water Proof", there is nothing about that speaker is even water resistant, never mind water proof. After taking it apart (to confirm it was water proof as advertised), I found 3 glaring faults:
1) There is no seal or gasket between the two halves, making it easy for water to wick in.
2) There is no moisture barrier between the paper speaker cone and the holes in the front of the plastic enclosure.
3) The wire feeds through a rather large hole, with a simple knot as a strain-relief (no rubber grommet to keep out water).

It's a blatant lie to call it "water proof". This is problematic for me because I wanted it incorporate it in my home intercom/PA system, but now I'm not so sure.

Granted, it's got a great price, but why lie about it?

title: READ THIS BEFORE PURCHASING
text:
Let me preface this by saying I'm a professional sports photographer who uses Canon photo equipment. When it works, it's great. However, there is a HUGE learning curve with this card. I had to scrap the instruction insert because, #1 it was written in broken and English, and two, it was EXTREMELY difficult to understand. I feel like the technology with this card is still in beta testing because it is definitely not for an everyday consumer to plug and play.

RULE #1 - DO NOT FORMAT WITH YOUR CAMERA. If you do, you'll lose the wireless connectivity, and you'll receive very vague, frustrating error codes. You MUST download the Toshiba software to "initialize" the card after each usage. I say "initialize" because that's the word the software uses instead of format.

RULE #2 - If your camera goes into sleep mode, you will lose connectivity, and the only way I've been able to retrieve it, is to turn the camera off, take the card out and reinsert it to re-establish connection. Once again, if you lose connectivity, you'll continually get error codes that your mobile device can't locate the card.

RULE #3 - Keep your mobile device pretty close to your camera while transferring. The slightest distance can make a HUGE impact on the transfer capability.

So, why is this card good? When it works, it works great. On my Samsung phone, I'm able to choose the photo I want, then share it via any app that'll work with photos such as Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, etc. Secondly, I was able to purchase two of these cards for less than one Eyefi card. Since I use this for sports, I only need to transfer photos in the event of a big play, so I don't need it to work constantly. I feel like this card is on the brink of being successful, but not quite. Hopefully there are still improvements being made.

title: Great for nature and getting started in astro
text:
Very clear, white light transparency. What I mean is, I couldn't detect any changes to the color or the contrast when looking through them. They DO take the Nikon and Barska tripod adapters. The little labeled knob in the front of the focus wheel unscrews and voila!

You get really great contrast and images. The zoom feature allows you to go wide for tracking a flock of birds or getting up close.

According to Patrick Moore's book Exploring the Night Sky with Binoculars the specs on these bino's would be right in the sweet spot for a starter pair, (he recommends a 7x50) though bigger objectives of course are better. You can _just_ start to make out the disk-shaped light of Saturn, but it's plenty bright. It's still tiny, but the color differences between planets is very clearly visible. It's also plenty bright for looking at the moon, but without a tripod you'll get a headache trying. You'll also be impressed by how many objects these binocular pulls in that are completely invisible to the naked eye, but keep your expectations realistic! You aren't going to initiate first contact with an alien race just because you have a zoom feature. :)

NEVER point your binoculars or telescope at the sun without the appropriate filter(s)!!

However, if you decide to use solar filters to view the sun, there's plenty of magnification here for our nearest star. To find filters that fit correctly you should know that the outer diameter of the objective is 55.6mm. The only models of quality binocular solar filters I could find that fit well were the Seymour Solar brand. You'll want the 2.5" set which works from 55 to 60mm OD, but I was not able to find these on Amazon. Of course, follow all the manufacturer's safety instructions.

title: Bose Companion 20 vs Bose Companion 2 Series III - Detailed Impressions
text:
The wonderful Bose Companion 2 Series 3 computer speakers have graced our home ever since they first came out. We have really enjoyed them. Not at the computer but instead for inconspicuous bookshelf speakers in a small room. the Speakers were souced wirelessly via an Apple Airport Express router and AirPlay. Though they were great for this function, recently I have been itching for an upgrade. So, the other day I visited a Bose store and came home with the larger and more expensive Companion 20 speakers. So, how do they compare? Here are some detailed impressions...

SOUND QUALITY OVERVIEW

The less expensive Companion 2 held up pretty well when first compared side-by-side with the 20s. In fact, at lower volumes the two speakers sounded nearly identical. After a while, the supiorority of the Companion 20's became clearly evident. They are much more rich and crisp than the 2s. After hours of listening to the new speakers I switched back to the 2's and they sounded tinny and shril. Especially at moderate and higher listening volumes.

HIGHS and LOWS

First about the lows. Again initial impression led me to think the base sounded nearly identical on both speakers. It wasn't until I played bass heavy music that I noticed the difference. The 20s bass is much tighter and gives a cleaner thump. In their promotional material Bose states that when one walks into a room where 20's are playing they will look around for a base module. This is true. Especial when the rear of the speakers are placed near a wall or a corner. My Companion 2s are spread nearly three feet apart on a bookshelf. Each speaker is slightly angled towards eachother with the backs up against the corners of the shelf. This is the sweet spot for the room. As to the high, the 20s are also the clear leader. Female voices SHINE on these silver speakers. High notes on the 2s by comparison sound like they are distant as though the singer is behind a closed door. In general every musical detail (highs, lows and mids) are better detailed and distinct. Play a song with complex instrumentation, for example, and you will distinctly hear most every nuance of each instrument. On the Companion 2 speakers similarly complex tracs sounded blended together where the details were muted or lost.

BUILD QUALITY

I thought the 2s were well built but, oh my goodness, they look like toys next to the aluminum 20 speakers! The quality becomes especially apparent when you feel the weight and heartiness of the build. This is best showcased by just the control module on the 20. The knob feels substantial and turns smoother than any dial I have ever used. Really, you must try it!. This buttery smoothness is balanced absolutely perfectly with proper resistance and responsiveness. The module further boasts a touch sensitive on/off "button" which is also amazingly responsive and instant. In short, looking at the Companion 20s and controlling them are just as pleasant as listening to them! The 2s are solidly built but their look and feel is only average.

FURTHER COMPARISONS

I own several othe Bose products including he Bose sound link mini, the QC20 in-ear headphones, and the Bose QC15 over-the-ear headphones. So, how does the sound of the Companion 20s compare to these other products?

Soundlink Color - The 20s win easily. This is remarkable because I think the Color sounded better than the Companion 2's eventhough the it is a small Bluetooth speaker compared to a wired 2 speaker system. The color has better clarity than the 2s and overall boast a higher fidelity. The 2s did have better stereo separation (obviously) and can play at a higher volume. On the other hand, my new Companion 20s just sound better than the Soundlink Color in every single aspect.

Quiet Comfort 20 - The similarity between the Quiet Comort 20 headphones and the Companion 20 computer speakers comes in warmth of sound. Both boast a warmth that is very pleasing and Senheiser like. This is where the comparisons end. The QC headphones win in the area that they sound a little more natural and balanced. Though, the Companion 20s beat the QC20s in crispness and detail. When I have a choice between the two, I enjoy listening to the speakers over the QC20 in-ear headphones.

Quiet Comfort 15 - Now, here is where the Companion 20s begin to fall short. The best sound I have ever heard comes from my QC15 headphones. They are astonishingly impressive. These companion 20's get me much closer to that great sound quality. In fact, the Companion 20s sound warmer and a tad richer than the QC15! Unfortunately, the music is not as detailed nor crisp. I do find myself debateing whether or not to enjoy music via the QC15 headphones or via the Companion 20 computer speakers. By comparison the Companion 2's always sounded decent but I never purposely chose to go listen to them over any of the other Bose products that I own.

CONCLUSION

Though Companion 2s have seen series of re-iterations through the years, the Companion 20s are still the original speakers first introduced in 2011. To me, the fact that a Companion 20 series 2 does not yet exist hints that there is not much to improve with the current speaker. Give these speakers a serious try and I think you will agree.

PS - A note about source volume. The manual for the 20s instructs to place the source volume at a maximum of 80 percent. This is key! Use the control pod to crank up the volume. There will be no distortion not even when turning the dial all the way up. With the 2s the sound the sound improved with the source volume at 100 percent and the knob on the speakers at slightly over half. All this to say that the more expensive 20's do a better job of signal processing and improving the source signal into that distinctive rich and Bose sound. By the way, the 20s top volume is about twice that of the 2s.

title: Very nice all-in-one
text:
I was skeptical about a Samsung branded PC, but gave it a try based on previous experience with the brand's kitchen appliances. For a hundred dollars less than other AIO brands, it's worth trying at this price, with a couple caveats.

I must say the image quality on the screen is fantastic, and while the design is a little strange the reason for it - a very capable built-in sound system - is worth it. The PC shipped securely packaged and setup was easy, although the typical multiple Windows updates that had to happen consumed 8 hours before I could actually use the thing. The 12Gb of supplied RAM makes operation nice and snappy. The only down-side is limited USB connectivity - although there are two USB 3.0 ports so adding a 3.0 port replicator was simple made things much more flexible, and beware this system has NO disc drive. So if you need to load software from CDROM or if you want to watch a disc-based movie you are out of luck unless you purchase an external drive. So, port replicator and external DVD drive and boom, there goes the $100 price differential.

Good wifi and BT built in, and gigabit Ethernet of course. The supplied chicklet keyboard is a joke, but at least it is wireless so it's convenient. If you do a lot of typing or keyboard-based gaming throw the chicklet thing away and upgrade to a real keyboard. Another added expense.

Overall a nice machine with a few shortcomings. They should have upped the price to the same as an HP and included a DVD drive and better keyboard.

We use feather pillows, so I can't cut out a place in a foam one, like somebody else did. Best I have been able to do was to loop up and tie off some excess cord a few inches from the speaker, then remove one one side of a binder clip to thread the cord through, re-attach the metal side/loop onto the binder clip, then clip to pillow inside the case. When the speaker slides down, the loop can't go through the binder clip loop. At least it keeps it roughly at the right distance from the top edge of the pillow. Still, there has to be a better way! Hope somebody else has some ideas.

Sounds a little tinny, and I only use it to listen to audiobooks as I fall asleep. Haven't tried it with music.

UPDATE Sept 2015: I've had this for about 6 months now, and use it every night, all night. I am very happy with it. I don't even need the battery to boost the sound level, which has a wide range, from very soft to strong. I keep it pretty soft, so that my husband doesn't hear it from his side of the bed, and use it 8 or more hours per night. This is much more comfortable than wearing headphones to sleep, which I had been doing. I was also worried about hearing damage from headphones, even at very soft levels. This can be used on top of a pillow, or even underneath a thin to medium thick one. And since I don't even need the battery for amplification, this is one less thing that I have to plug in and re-charge. I am increasing my my rating from 4 to 5 stars, since I have had 6 months to give it a good trial.

title: Why I Chose 2015 MacBook
text:
My 2011 MacBook Air has been a fantastic companion. It has everything I needed to do my work and nothing I didn't need. It was a great combination of size, price, performance and usability. But after three-plus years, it is time to choose a successor.

My method to pick my everyday computer is pretty straight forward: Set my critera, choose candidate models, and then narrow down the list to one. The 2015 MacBook was announced while I was going thru this process. At first glance, it did not seem that the new MacBook would be a candidate. It seemed pricey, it was a first-gen model, and it looked fragile. But after playing with it at the Apple Store, I saw no reason to eliminate it from the list.

My criteria for the replacement was simple: I needed a mid-sized computer (no 11-inch or 15-inch models), 8GB RAM (this is a must-have), in the $1200 range (to match my $1/day computer budget), with an all-day battery (no charging required for at least 8 hours of usage). These were all hard requirements. Other nice-to-have options were Retina display (but I can live with non-Retina), 256GB storage (though I can make-do with 128GB) and lighter the better.

You may have noticed that matching some arbitrary performance benchmarks was not a requirement. That's because any and all of the current generation Apple computers are more than sufficient to accomplish my daily tasks: Firefox for Web Browsing, Word and Excel for documents and spreadsheets, Photoshop & Lightroom for viewing and editing photos, and XCode along with some Terminal tools for development work. In fact, I could have continued to use my 4-year old MacBook Air for these tasks were it not for its 4GB RAM and (now puny) 4-hour battery.

After a little bit of browsing on the Apple online store, I chose the following computers for my list (all prices are from the Educational Store and without tax/shipping):

Model Price RAM Storage Battery Display Weight
13" Air 1039 8GB 128GB 12 Hrs. Non 2.5 lbs
13" Pro 1199 8GB 128GB 10 Hrs. Retina 3.0 lbs
13" Air 1239 8GB 256GB 12 Hrs. Non 2.5 lbs
12" Macbook 1249 8GB 256GB 9 Hrs. Retina 2.0 lbs
13" Pro 1399 8GB 256GB 10 Hrs. Retina 3.0 lbs

The next few steps were just a process of elimination. First, I removed the outliers: The 13" Pro ($1399) was far outside my budget and therefore the first to go. The 13" Air (for $1039) had its low price as an advantage, but since others offered more while meeting the budget, it was also eliminated. The new list now looked like this:

Model Price RAM Storage Battery Display Weight
13" Pro 1199 8GB 128GB 10 Hrs. Retina 3.0 lbs
13" Air 1239 8GB 256GB 12 Hrs. Non 2.5 lbs
12" Macbook 1249 8GB 256GB 9 Hrs. Retina 2.0 lbs

I could also eliminate the Price and RAM criteria now, since all models were 8GB and price variation was less than 5%:

Model Storage Battery Display Weight
13" Pro 128GB 10 Hrs. Retina 3.0 lbs
13" Air 256GB 12 Hrs. Non 2.5 lbs
12" MacBook 256GB 9 Hrs. Retina 2.0 lbs

So the decision really came down to the nice-to-have options. The 13" Pro gets a +1 for Retina, 13" Air gets a +1 for 256GB storage, but the MacBook gets +2 for having both Retina and 256GB. On top of that, it is the lightest of all candidates (another +0.5 maybe?). I think we have a clear winner!

Now, how to choose between Silver, Gold and Space Grey?

text: I'm on the fence about this camera, but went with four rather than three stars because, to be fair, it will be good for most occasions for most people.  I take a lot of pictures of archaeological sites and artifacts.  It is wonderful for archaeological sites -- which means, for general outdoor photography.  It handles extreme brightness and low light very well.  It sees better in dark recesses than my own eyes do. :)  But it just can't seem to handle close-ups well, even in "close-up" or "macro" modes.  A bust, sure.  A coin, very difficult.  And it can't negotiate shooting through glass -- not in a museum case and so, I would guess, not through a window.  I'm keeping it, as it really did fine for about 90% of my pictures, but I will have to continue to carry a second camera into museums and the like. (If I'm missing something here that will solve my issues, PLEASE let me know.  I'd be delighted to find the way to make this work for all my photo needs!)

title: Very nice kit, great price.
text:
The very first thing you should do when you get a DJI Phantom drone is get a filter kit. Even before you get the Phantom, get the filter kit. The reason for this is that the Phantom lens comes totally unprotected. Yes, it comes with a lens, but you don't want to mess that one up. Remove that one, stick it in the original DJI box, and then use these. The glass filters in this kit will do a good job of protecting the glass of the lens, and they'll significantly enhance the images you capture. The UV filter is perfect for protecting and not changing the image you capture.

The other lenses that come in this kit are a circular polarizer, which reduced glare, ND4, which reduces the amount of light that comes in (think shooting towards a sunrise) and an ND8, which further reduces the amount of light that enters into the lens.

The whole setup comes with a very nice nylon carrying case that has a velcro lip to shut it.

For the money, this is a very nice kit.

I was fortunate enough to buy this at a discount. The price does not influence my feedback or review. This is my personal experience, feedback and honest opinion of this product, whether it be good or bad. If this review has been helpful, please kindly click YES, or if I've left anything out, feel free to ask. I rely heavily on reviews, photos and experiences when I make my decision to buy a product online and I will only leave a fair, HONEST and unbiased review of each product. I will not deceive anyone or mislead about any product. I would also love to know if I'm meeting those needs and answering any questions you may have in this review or if I need to add anything.

title: Issues after only 3 months, and 7 months in the battery is depleted. Never had this happen before on a laptop.
text:
*UPDATE*
After 7 months, I cannot unplug the laptop. The battery says 95% and charging, but if I ever unplug it then it turns off instantly. I had a $200 dell before this that was a better laptop than this piece of junk. Waste of money. I cannot believe amazon puts the 5 star reviews first and neglects ones like mine that have had issues with the quality control on this laptop. It is very rare that I ever give a 1 star, or a 5 star review and try to remain neutral, but on this purchase, I feel like I wasted $600.

I started out with a 4 star review about 3 months ago, but now it is one star.

I am having keyboard backlight issues, as well as the screen brightness flickering. Also, you cannot choose the dedicated gpu. It defaults to intels graphics instead. This renders the geforce gpu totally useless. I have found a workaround, to relieve some stress from the cpu, but I had to force rename apps and a bunch of other things as well. Like VLC, I had to rename to VLC1 and select it in the geforce menu to always use the gpu instead of intels graphics.

Overall, I knew I should have just saved and built my own computer. I hate laptops. So problematic and they always run hot. But given the issues I am starting to have only 3 months into this one... what a waste.

Save your money and get a decent laptop if you need one. Go with a new one that has at least a 10 series gpu like a 1050ti or 1060, and a real i5, not a hyperthreaded 2 core i5 like this one. You can spend a couple hundred more and get so much better quality. I do not recommend this laptop anymore, the bang for the buck has gone right out of the window when stupid little issues keep happening. Also, 1080p on a 15" screen is way too much. Text size needs to be bigger and the dpi is default to 125%, which makes everything pixelated and crappy looking. So if you are going to default the dpi to 125%, why not just give us a 720p laptop? After I set the dpi to normal, I could barely read text in folder and for chrome, I had to increase text size to large and zoom to 115%... what a waste. But the dpi by default and all the acer junk along with it, horrible planning.

title: They do what I wanted.
text: I ordered these for a new Energy Take Classic 5.1 surround sound speaker system. It took some thinking but they ended up working just fine when I mounted the speakers upside down with the "L" bracket that screws onto the stand, after removing the plastic hanger bracket from the speaker. If you try to do it right side up, you can't use banana plugs on the wires, not enough room, but you could just leave off the plugs and they'd mount fine right side-up. I give 'em 5 stars because any stands you get will need mounting modification since there are so many satellite speakers on the market. These are nice & heavy and conceal the 14/2 wiring just fine. I don't understand the multiple comments on having trouble feeding the wire thru the stand. I used new 14/2 wire, cut ends only, and threaded it down from the top in long lengths. Just leaning the stand over while I did this let the wire slip right out through the bottom without me even needing to pull on the exit wire. I can only imagine that the wire draw problems are from pre-wired plug ends in place. If so, try tying a lead wire to feed those. It might help. If you tried to feed the wire from the bottom of the stand, no wonder you had problems. You could even leave the tubes unassembled to feed the shorter runs and then thread it all together. No danger of these stands tipping over. At $30/pair, I think they're a solid investment and are the little brother of microphone stands in quality. I bought 2 sets.

title: The Future...
text:
Samsung NX1 first impressions

From the very first instance upon opening the box, Samsung has made the NX1 a special treat. It isn’t a normal box that opens from the top but more like opening a woman’s facial powder box that has a top to lift off. There is a very special feel about opening the NX1.

Holding the NX1 you immediately feel that it is a substantial and serious camera. There are new buttons and dials that will challenge even the most experienced Samsung user, so as with any new camera a certain learning curb and patience is required. The NX1 works fast and smoothly without an lag time. The NX1 is a substantial photographic tool, excellent ergonomics, a bit hefty and heavy when using the 50-200mm lens, nice wide camera strap. Nice to have the pop up flash for fill flash.

Battery life is outstanding and can go for close to 400 photos.

I shot in custom mode in both b/w and color (one has to save a copy of a photo specifically associated with the custom mode you are trying to save (the trash symbol is the save button…took me a while to figure that one out!).

Gone is the micro mini sd card and now a regular sd memory card is used.

ONE GETS A SENSE WHILE SHOOTING WITH THE NX1 THAT THE CAMERA IS WORKING WITH YOU AS A THIRD EYE AND THE VERY EXTENSION OF ONE’S PHOTOGRAPHIC ABILITIES. THE NX1 SEEMS TO BE CONSCIOUS TO A CERTAIN DEGREE OF WHAT IS GOING ON IN THE SCENE AND QUICKLY SIZES UP THE MOMENT, BRINGING TO RESOLUTION AN EXCELLENT IMAGE.

Though having all the many features of the earlier NX series, the NX1 is clearly for advanced users with plenty of room to grow and expand one’s abilities. The price is expensive but in the months to come should drop a bit.

title: This will harm your records.

This piece of junk is just a piece of cloth. If you can't find one of the old types to use, you would be better off using nothing at all, literally. This one will just push dust down deeper into the grooves. Some dishonest floundering mid-level executive at RCA or whoever is making this lie of a product thought "we can make thousands and thousands of dollars peddling what is fifteen cents of materials for $15", by fooling people into thinking they are buying the old product that they came to trust. This is my only Amazon review after using Amazon for many years, and it may be my last, but I could not let this rip off go uncalled.

title: Unique, and still pretty classy. I love it!
text:
If you're looking at this case, you've probably seen that video on youtube of it in action. If you haven't, I highly recommend it!

Aesthetically, the Inwin 915 offers you something different, while still being elegant. On the outside, it's massive, easily dwarfing my beloved Inwin 805 that my other computer resides in. The core is made out of steel, which unfortunately makes it a bit heavy. The exterior is bead blasted aluminum everywhere except the side panel trim, which is brushed aluminum. When you power on your computer, the top opens up. When you turn it off, the top closes. Kinda neat. The mechanism to do so is actually a belt drive system, which.. is a bit noisy unfortunately.

Above the front bezel, but below the IO ports, is a very thin line of RGB LEDs that you can control with your motherboard's ARGB header. Unfortunately, Inwin doesn't tell you how many LEDs are in that, so... yeah.. actually, Inwin doesn't tell you anything because a manual is not included in the box!

Installing parts inside the case is fairly easy! The space between the right side panel and the motherboard tray is wide enough to not require any serious cable management, and the Inwin logos screen printed all over the right side panel do a great job hiding that mess if you decide you're too excited to bother with cable management. There's room for 8 140mm fans (3 on top, 3 on the front, 2 on the bottom), and 1 120MM fan (on the back, next to the motherboard). Unfortunately, if you use the bottom 2 fan slots for 140mm fans like I did, and your motherboard has headers for front USB and such on the bottom like mine did, running cables between the fans and the motherboard gets a little tricky. Oh yeah, and if you put 140MM fans on the bottom, you cannot mount your GPU vertically.

So, for such a massive case, it's a little bit smaller inside than you'd hope. There's room for a massive power supply and several 3.5" hard drives, but doing a push-pull fan configuration on your water cooling would be annoying. You can fit a truly massive video card in there though - even my Zotac Amp Extreme has a ton of room to spare! As easy as the side panels are to remove, I'm puzzled that Inwin chose to hold the front and rear panels on with screws. They are hinged and swing open, but you have 2 captive thumbscrews that need to be tightened to keep them closed. I wish Inwin considered using magnets instead - it would look better.

As for thermals, I haven't really had time to form an opinion about them yet. It definitely breathes a lot better than my Inwin 805 does, so there's that!

Finally, let's talk about the price. You're paying a premium for this case because Inwin hasn't made that many of them. If you look at their other oddball cases, they offer nothing more and cost twice as much. It's still a really solid, really well built case that should last years.

There are a couple of downsides, which is to be expected. The watch straps are proprietary which can be a pain. Another downside, is that since it is proprietary, there are very few apps when compared to Android or IOS, however I know Tinzen currently has more of the wearables market than Android. So, I look for there to start being more apps developed.

title: DSL-101 VS. DSL-102 lens EXHANGE case
text:
This review is try to clear up some of the possible confusion of which exchange case is which.
It appears that some of the Amazon videos are not for the correct products
Some earlier reviews could possibly be for the other case(s) as well.
First, let me clarify both of these lens cases are designed specifically to facilitate the removal and replacement of two lenses while out in a field situation, not support a camera body or more equipment.

I will try to point out the major differences in the DSL-101 and the DSL-102 in an attempt to remove any misunderstanding between the two cases.
1. the DSL-101 will fit a [Canon] zoom lens up to 250mm vs. 300mm and larger for the DSL-102.
2. the DSH-101 has a Velcro closure vs. a zipper on the DSL-102.
3. the DSL-101 has one outer storage pocket for a lens cap, SD card, et cetera and one Velcro closure inner compartment vs. two larger storage pockets on the DSL-102, but one of these carries the waterproof cover, (the DSL-101 has a dedicated small storage compartment under the belt fastener for the rain hood).
4. the DSL-101 has a convenient belt loop fastener on the backside and a thin width shoulder strap for carrying the case vs. a wide padded shoulder strap and a nice carry handle on the top of the case for the larger DSL-102.

title: A really solid performing and affordable 2-in-1!
text:
I bought this computer over 5 months ago when my old one final gave up on me. I did a lot of research before purchasing this and I can say that, so far, I am really pleased. I didn't really need a 2-in-1 per se, and with its 15.6 inch screen this might not be something one uses on a daily basis. Having said that, the touchscreen functionality is really nice and it is pretty seamless when switching over from keyboard functionality (which is beautifully backlit,btw). The 3 modes - laptop, tent and tablet- are convenient and you don't get the feeling that the hinges would break,unlike a few other models out there. The chassis has nice, sturdy feel to it- not cheap and plastic-y. The trackpad is easy to use. I like that it is just slightly off-center. Also, can I just say 'huzzah!' to Acer for not sacrificing USB ports! I use this for work and the available ports really make a big difference.
At 4.5+ lbs it is a bit heftier than, say, MacBook, which is also considerably more expensive, or HP Specter. And, unlike with HP, you don't feel the fan constantly rumbling or the heat rising under your wrists as you type. For me, that's super important since I need to write a lot. When the fan does kick in, it doesn't sound like a heavy tanker but more like a delux jet engine taxing on a runway (or that's how I imagine it to be). I can deal with that, especially since it's occasional rather than a constant. The 1080 HD screen is a really nice; images and colors are crisp- loads sharper than the Lenovo Flex or Yoga, which I tested at a computer store. I can't speak for gaming, but streaming videos are great. I am not blown-over by speakers' sound quality which is just average despite boasting Dolby Audio. But, then again, when it comes to laptops, especially at this price-range few speakers really impress regardless if they're using Bang&Olulfsen quad speakers or Harman Kardon. Using earbuds or pluging it to external speakers will probably up the overall sound quality. title: Can get very tightly stuck in Neutrik combo XLR/TS jacks.
text:
I did not purchase this on Amazon, however I own this exact adapter (see the included picture). Beware that if you intend to connect this adapter to a combo XLR/TS jack such as a high quality Neutrik combo XLR/TS jack (found on many good quality digital audio interfaces such as my Focusrite Saffire Pro 40 audio interface) this adapter's TS connectors may stick in the Neutrik jack so tight that you may not be able to remove them despite applying significant force. This appears to be due to the tips of these TS connectors being shaped in such a way that there is a pronounced sharp curve rather than a gradual curve in the groove between the ring and the tip itself.

I was able to figure out how to remove this without sending my audio adapter in to a professional for repair. I opened up my Saffire Pro 40 and from the inside I was able to access the back-side of the Neutrik combo jack. The Neutrik combo jack has a slot through which you can see the tip of the stuck 1/4" male TS connector. Through this same slot you can see the part (a prong) of the Neutrik jack that holds the jack in place. Intuitively it would seem that you would simply move the prong (such as by prying it with the tip of a jeweler's screw driver) directly away from the tip, however in practice that doesn't actually work. What *does* work is if you use the jeweler's screwdriver to put a bit of pressure on the prong so that it's torqued a bit *sideways* (rather than directly away from the TS connector), as you simultaneously attempt to remove the TS connector. The connector will then come loose.

I have noticed on various forums that other folks have had issues with this Hosa adapter qand Neutrik combo jacks. I also found a great alternative which works perfeclty. It's the Sescom SES-IPOD-XLRM06 3.5mm Stereo to Dual XLR Male Mono Audio Cable.

To Hosa: Please change the way you shape the groove near the tip of the TS connectors so that the curvature is more smooth and gradual.
