title: I like the Bluetooth 4.0 one and recommend it
text:
It is confusing that Amazon puts the Bluetooth 4.0 and 2.1 reviews together. There are major differences between the two.

I got the Bluetooth 4.0 one. I like it and I recommend it. I use it with the Apple EarPods that came with the iPhone for the sound and comfort. I have tried other Bluetooth earphones but almost all of them use replaceable rubber plugs, which are uncomfortable for me and fall out easily, and I have not been happy with the sound quality of the ones I have tried. It does not respond to the EarPods' mic or remote control (answer and volume buttons) but that is a minor issue, since the unit has its own controls and mic. When I ride my bike, the sound drops out occasionally, more than the Sony SBH20, but not more than others I tried (e.g., the Motorola S9-HD). Cupping your palm over it may be enough to cut off the connection, but the signal is often strong enough to maintain a connection when I am on one floor above or below.

What I really like is that it can pair with multiple (2) devices at the same time (e.g., laptop, phone) and play the active source automatically, without having to manually disconnect one and reconnect the other. You hear only one source at a time though, not the mixed sound of both. I don't think my other Bluetooth unit does that. To pair with multiple masters, first pair with one master (e.g., a phone), then disable Bluetooth on the first master, which will let you pair it with the second master (e.g., a laptop), and go back to the first master and re-enable Bluetooth, which will reconnect with the jumbL. There is a limit of pairing with two hosts simultaneously. I tried various combinations of more than two hosts (computer, phone, etc) but it doesn't seem to want to pair with more than two. The Sony SBH20 (Bluetooth 3) can also pair with two devices at a time, but the factory default is to pair with one (to save power) and you have to explicitly enable it. After extensive use, the JumbL may fail to reconnect to either or both hosts after 1-2 weeks. Power cycling could solve the problem, but once every 3-4 weeks you may need to tell the host to forget the device and re-discover and re-pair with it.

Mine (4.0, not 2.1) uses Micro USB for charging, as does the Sony SBH20. I have read many other reviews that complain about the use of a proprietary USB charging cable (on the Bluetooth 2.1 ones) rather than Micro USB. The 4.0 with MicroUSB can also charge and continue to work at the same time, unlike the 2.1. Charging from empty to full seems pretty quick.

Siri works, although it can be a little tricky. You have to hold the button for about 1.5 to 2 seconds, release the button, and wait for 2-3 seconds after releasing the button for the Siri beep before you talk. For over a month I did not know I could use Siri, because on the iPhone, you hear the Siri beep while the button is still held. One common mistake is that you hold the button for too long (3 seconds) and the JumbL shuts down instead of bringing up Siri. On the Sony SBH20, I have not figured out how to use Siri by pressing holding the corresponding button.

I think it is definitely worth the extra $5 to get the Bluetooth 4.0 one, especially given the recent price drop.

Update:

After a little over 6 months, the battery on my unit stops charging. It still works when plugged in, but it would not show the charging LED (red when charging, blue when fully charged) when plugged in to USB. It is a little disappointing... but I have used it pretty heavily every day (I wear it for several hours a day every day). Most of the time I just plugged it to my computer's USB port and had no problems, but I noticed that it stopped charging when I plugged it to an external charger. I am not sure if the charger had a problem (too much current?) that may have killed it? because it looks more like a charging circuitry problem, rather than the battery itself.

Comparison with the Sony SBH20

Since my JumbL stopped charging, I have been using the Sony SBH20, which uses Bluetooth 3 rather than Bluetooth 4 and comes with a pair of ear buds. Both can pair with two devices at the same time, which is important for me. The Sony SBH20 one has a power switch, whereas JumbL relies on the multi-purpose button for play/pause/answer/siri/pair/power. SBH20 can mute the microphone by double-clicking but I always feel unsure if I have done it correctly and have always gone back to the phone to mute it. The Sony SBH20 also charges with MicroUSB but has a dust cover, which I appreciate and is nicely built and has not fallen off yet after about 5 months. I like the Sony SBH20's metal clip, which is much more robust than the plastic clip of the JumbL and can rotate. SBH20 also supports NFC pairing but I have not used it. However, I often press the wrong buttons for FF/REW or Vol+/-. Sony's volume buttons control the unit's volume locally, whereas the Jumbo's volume buttons control the volume on the host (which seems more intuitive to me) over Bluetooth. Another thing is the SBH20 does not seem to report its battery level to the host device (instead, it uses the blinking LED's color) but the JumbL does. I have grown to like the SBH20 hardware very much but I still prefer the JumbL's firmware.

title: Perfect running companion, very lightweight & feature rich.
text:
After trying to use my Samsung Gear S2 smartwatch as a running watch I ultimately determined that it wasn't cut out for the task. I landed on the Polar M430 after comparing all the competition from Garmin, TomTom, etc. The Polar won me over because of its price and ease of use AND their software suite. Feature for feature this watch has everything most runners will need. It locks in to GPS SUPER fast which is great on cold dark mornings. The interface is easy and straightforward and provides a great deal of information on the oblong screen. It took me a while to figure out how to get the backlight to stay lit, and that's probably the one complaint that I have about the watch. Really take some time to read through the features offered vs. the competition and I think most people will find that the Polar is the best choice.

I was pleasantly surprised that it does cadence measurements without needing a foot pod! After doing research on why cadence is important, I was really hoping to find this feature without needing to buy a separate foot pod, and I think that the Polar was the only one that offered it on the watch without needing a foot pod.

title: Rough start but got it working.
text:
Had a bit of a rough start getting the cam to work properly with my freshly updated Windows 10 machine. However, I did get it working and it's going to do exactly what I need it to do.
1) plug cam in and wait for the windows drivers to load up.
2) Open up the 'camera' app and noticed a really wicked flicker that didn't get better with any settings.
3) download and install the Logitech software that controls the pan and zoom and stuff.
4) Notice no picture at all comes out of the cam anymore.
5) reboot and fiddle with crap that did nothing. Undo the crap and reboot, still in condition above.
6) uninstall the device from 'device manager'
7) reboot
8) plug camera in again and wait for several minutes while Windows figures out what to do.
9) open camera software, everything is perfect.
10) open logitech software, everything is perfect.
11) play with settings, do a test video, everything is perfect.

Also, put the camera on a short tripod and point it straight down to see how it does taking pix of a phone for demos. The auto-focus is focusing in the wrong spot, but when I adjust the manual focus I can get a great picture with the camera about 8 inches off the desktop.

So, I would take off points for not being 'plug and play' exactly, but I was able to get it to work without much fuss. And it's going to be a great camera for my purposes (online testing) and my daughter's (Youtubing).

title: A step in the right direction for laptops
text:
I own the 15" version of this laptop with 16GB ram, and I find it to be amazing. If you want a compact, lightweight laptop with many of the features of a traditional 15" laptop without sacrificing battery life, this is it! I am switching from a MacBook Air 13" after using it exclusively for the last 5 years.

Here are all the pros of this laptop compared to the MacBook Air (Current Gen, i7 256GB):
+ Lighter weight (2.7 lb vs 3.0 lb)
+ Bigger screen (15.0" vs 13.3")
+ Higher resolution (1080p vs 1440x900)
+ Better Display Color (95% vs 60% sRGB)
+ IPS display
+ Outdoor mode that significantly boosts the brightness of the display
+ Display has anti-reflective coating
+ Thin bezels -> similar display cover size compared to Air's (13.7"x9.03" vs 12.8"x8.94")
+ Thinner than MacBook Air at its thickest point (0.61" vs 0.68")
+ Dedicated GPU (Nvidia 940MX, 2GB DDR3)
+ Double the RAM (16GB vs 8GB)
+ Exchangeable M.2 SSD (I upgraded it to 1TB, cloning recommended)
+ Fingerprint Reader
+ USB-C with Thunderbolt 3
+ Extra USB port
+ Full-sized HDMI port
+ Support for Multiple Displays (without daisy chaining)
+ Quieter fans
+ Extra keys (e.g. Prt Src, Insert, Delete, Home, Pg Up, Pg Dn, End)
+ Faster RAM (DDR4, 2133MHz vs. DDR3, 1600MHz)
+ Faster SSD (NVMe vs AHCI)
+ Faster i7 processor (2.7 vs 2.2GHz)
+ Better integrated Graphics (Intel HD 620 vs 6000)
+ Bigger battery (66 vs 54 Whr)
+ Only $50 more expensive ($1399 vs $1349)

Here are the cons of this laptop compared to the MacBook Air:
- Magnesium Alloy encasing is less rigid (but doesn't flex under normal use)
- Has a MicroSD slot, not a full sized SD slot
- No MagSafe power port (although charging through a magnetic USB-C connector should work)

I feel like the keyboard takes a little bit of getting used to (keys feel looser than MacBook Air keys), but after a while I learn to comfortably type quickly on it.

Also, the trackpad feels great. Basically, just as sensitive as a MacBook trackpad.

Overall, I think it is fair to say that the battery life, trackpad, keyboard, keyboard backlighting, webcam, and operating system are functionally equivalent to those on the MacBook Air. You can also lift the display with one hand, just like you can do on Macbooks!

By the way, the battery life of the 15" version is good: ~10 hrs with normal usage, including web browsing, document editing, and youtube videos at 60% display brightness. You may be able to get even more battery life with battery saver settings enabled.

I think if you just look at all the pros compared to cons, it's obvious that this laptop is the clear winner. I am comfortably writing this review from my LAP on a 15" screen with NO fatigue, a feat I previously thought unimaginable. I am quite happy with this product :D

title: Great little camera module for PI
text:
Great little camera module for PI. The image quality is very nice, despite the cheap M12 lens. It's very easy to use, just make sure you insert the ribbon cable facing the right way and make sure it's seated straight and deep before you lock the connector on the PI board. This camera is good in low light, only problem is that you have to sacrifice all your frame rate to do it unless you add IR illumination to the scene. This brings me to the only two things I don't like about the camera:

1) It's as if they built this thing specifically to satisfy people that HATE noise in a picture. I get it, people want quality, but HACKERS want ability. I'm not saying that it should be rebuilt with very high gain amplification so that it runs like a demon in the dark and everything looks grainy... I'm saying it would be awfully nice to have a version of this camera that had higher amplification on the sensor so that it could perform more aggressively in very low light. The ELP USBFHD01 cameras behave like this, allowing you to reduce gain dramatically for low noise, or bump it up all the way for surprisingly high framerates in awful lighting. Sometimes you just really want to see motion and noise isn't as important.

2) That short little ribbon cable... sigh. The cable is a scant 5" long, so whatever you are doing for your project, you're pretty much sticking your PI right in there. It's ok, I suppose. I mean the Pi 3b has inbuilt WiFi and all so you can just about stick it anywhere, but still. Sometimes you want some cable length, and this just doesn't have it.

One thing I really do like about this cam, that I'd like to share with the world:

If you pass THIS to the camera, you can do some pretty interesting things for astronomy applications:

raspistill -q 100 -w 2592 -h 1891 -ISO 3200 -ss 5000000 -ex sports -t 10000 -o longexp.jpg

-q drives the image quality to 100%
-w and -h specify the capture resolution.2592 x 1944 maxes this camera out, important for pinpoints like stars. I used 1891 for the height to push it to wider aspect but still avoiding the zoom in effect that happens at wider angle aspects. Try 1920x1080 to see what I mean.
-ISO 3200 tells it to push the gain on the camera all the way. This is a bit past the specs of the cam to make sure it milks everything it can get.
-ss specifies framerate in microseconds. I played with this value A LOT under dark sky tests and found that 5,000,000 microseconds was pretty much the max limit.
-ex sports sets the capture to "sports mode", which is suprisingly important. It pushes performance out of the camera like none of the other modes can.
-t 10000 forces the camera to time out and take the picture after ten seconds. I found that I could eliminate this and do fine. Increasing it does nothing for me.
-o of course specifies the output filename

Using this you'll get some noise but quite a lot of stars in capture, and since it's quite long, it's good for meteor trails as long as they are reasonably bright. The NOIR version of the cam really helps with that since it picks up on very hot objects especially well.

Anyway, it's a really great cam when used properly, and an EXCELLENT compliment for the RPI-Cam Interface program. Makes one badass little security cam / wildlife monitor. :-)

Rick NR417

title: If looks don't matter, do yourself a favor!
text:
These are, without a doubt, the best fans I've ever used. I've used Phanteks, Noctua, BeQuiet!, Corsair (from up and down each MFG's range). Pretty much everything but Gentle Typhoons. And these beat every single one of them... If your priorities lean towards balanced acoustic and cooling performance, rather than aesthetics.

I mean, the blades are dark green, semitranslucent, and incompatible with most build themes. The low noise adapters have white connectors and are not sleeved (but will likely be tucked behind the MB tray in your cable management area). So if you're building a sleek, sexy tempered glass show rig, these might not be for you.

If, however, you're hardly ever going to look at them, and prefer a clean, dark, impermeable sort of case (think Fractal), you won't find a better balance of airflow and acoustics. I don't know if they produce enough static pressure to penetrate a radiator, but they produce enough to create damned fine airflow in an intake-restrictive case. Good enough airflow, even with the low noise adapters (7V constant), that my 95W i5-2500 is being cooled by a NoFan CR-80EH (completely passive!) cooler inside a Fractal Design Define Mini C without ever getting over 72C under a substantial BOINC crowd-computing load for over 5 hours! And they do that in dead silence. No, really. Dead silence! I can hear the hum from my speakers (already quietened by ground loop noise isolators!), but not these fans (@ 7V).

title: Good fit and sound quality, mute button must be held down to activate
text:
I have used Plantronics headsets for my portable phones for many years. They stopped making the one I like, and though I have tried several different brands, I'd never found a satisfactory replacement. Well, now my Plantronics headsets are actually needing to be replaced, so I had to find something else.

I want a volume control, mute button, snug fit on the head, and a boom mic that doesn't transmit a lot of rubbing noise if you happen to touch it while you're talking. Oh, and I want good sound quality in my ear, and for the person on the other end of the call.

This Panasonic headset is just about perfect. I can talk on the phone and walk around, or put laundry into the dryer, and it stays on my head. The volume is adjustable, the boom doesn't transmit annoying sounds, and both ends of the call have good quality sound. The mute button is the only disappointment. It must be held down to mute the sound - doesn't stay on. That is a problem if I'm on a conference call and have a long period of time just listening. I mute so that a cough or sneeze doesn't annoy others. I decided that I can live with this, because I do have the choice of muting on the phone.

In all, I think I have found my replacement for my old Plantronics headsets.

title: EXTREMELY DISAPPOINTED - NOTHING TO BOAST OR CHERISH ABOUT
text:
To begin with I am no audiophile. The only thing I have is an ardent zeal for good music. I had Nokia WH 205 which died last week. I was very more than happy with them. Great lows, mids and highs. Again, the output also depend on the quality of the audio file played. Both ear pieces went dead for no reason all of a sudden. They lasted good, two years. I was going over the internet for a more nicer pair. I stumbled across Sony MDR-XB50AP. After going through the reviews, I bought it. It didn't excite me as much as my older Nokia WH-205, given the price. XB50AP cost me $35.99. I was like, 'what the heck'. I wasn't satisfied and went over various other reviews from wirecutter to cnet for quality in-ear headphones. My price bracket was until $50. While I was going over, I came across XB90EX. It was beyond my budget. Still, I thought there should be something with these as most of the reviewers have told. I also was under the impression that a higher priced product always is worth the money. So, I went ahead and bought them. I got them today. Boy, the package was awesome. The build was wow! I quickly put that in to listen to a track, I had the shock of my life. They are so so so dull in comparsion with XB50AP. I switched between both headphones on the same track that was running. At last, I AM HIGHLY DISAPPOINTED. The volume level was same. If I increased volume one level, it matched the sound of XB50AP. Yet, it only matched, there was no alarming EXTRA BASS as the packing box says nor anything extra ordinary give the price. They are good, but not worth $$.

The XB50AP are very good over XB90EX. They are also a tad better than Nokia WH-205. I haven't done a listening comparison with WH-205 and XB50AP. I would do that next and if my ears are not able to feel a difference I would stick to my old favorite WH-205.

My apologies to those who love this product. I didn't mean to hurt your sentiments. However, these didn't pull me to the edge of my seat nor leave my mouth wide apart. EXTREMELY DISAPPOINTED.

title: Trouble Free Installation
text:
I had a trouble free installation with this adapter, Azio BTD-V401

Asrock Z87 Extreme4 Motherboard / Windows 8.1 Pro

Plugged it into one of the USB 3.0 ports of the motherboard. Windows 8.1 automatically detects the adapter and installed the bluetooth driver. So far so good.

Downloaded CSR_Harmony_2 driver from Azio's website. Installation took about a minute and a half. Didn't need to reboot but did it anyways. No conflicts or problems with all my other installed devices.

No trouble with pairing the SONY MDR-1RBTMK2 Bluetooth Headphone. AptX Logo pops up when connecting. The light blinks rapidly 3 times on the headphone indicating aptX mode when playing music.

Set Bluetooth Audio Renderer under Windows Playback Devices as default and sound is sent to the headphone. This step is key to getting aptX mode working correctly. Turning the headphone off and Windows defaults back to my soundcard. Turn the headphone back on again, wait a few seconds for bluetooth to reconnect, and sound goes back to the headphone automatically.

So I'm very happy with my purchase and would recommend it to anyone interested in aptX. The Azio BTD-V401 adapter and CSR Harmony driver (although old and dated 2012), did not have any issues with Windows 8.1 Pro. If you have this OS with all the latest updates installed, I imagine your installation would be trouble free too.

Summary:

- in this price range there might be a lot better headsets if you have alternatives (not a fixed portfolio as me)

title: Unfortunately, it behooves one to read the specs on these devices
text:
Unfortunately, it behooves one to read the specs (not available here on amazon) of this product before purchase. I didn't and I am sorry. Here is why:
If you go to the manufacturer/vendor site there is a published spec:
STANDARD RECOMMENDED DRIVING IMPEDANCE 600Ω

When I put these in the signal path of my line level input to my amp, it did reduce the overall volume BUT it muffles the highs! I noticed this effect immediately. When I adjust the volume up to normal level the highs are definitely reduced and out of balance compared to frequency balance without the attenuators.

So then I checked the specs of my DAC and sure enough, it does NOT have 600Ω output impedance, not even close! Musical Fidelity VDAC-1 has output impedance of max 78Ω and actually under 50Ω for most of the frequency range.

So although these do lower the signal to the amp and allow me to use a more easily controllable range on my preamp volume control, I will be tossing these in the junk bin. I can't tolerate the change in frequency response they cause.

Probably I should add that I am driving the amp direct from the DAC, there is no active preamp between the DAC and the amp input (just a passive volume control which I have to set almost to the very lowest setting, which is why I wanted the passive attenuators).

And the DAC has lower impedance output probably than an active preamp...

title: Surprisingly great
text:
-------
Update June 4th, 2017: just a quick note to say that I've replaced this tile with the new Tile Mate for my cat, but I kept this old one for my purse just because (why send it in to be "recycled" if it's still working, right?). 18 months in and it's still working great. Will update again when the battery runs out.
*edit: this tile finally went to tile heaven as of Jan2018. That's over 2 years!
--------

I bought this as a pet tracker even though they don't necessarily recommend it for that use. I have a cat that tends to wander off but never very far. I figured with a 100 foot radius + me walking around enough I'd be able to track her down.

I tested it like crazy with all her usual hiding spots to make sure it'd work for me and that I wouldn't have to return it and was very impressed with the range. I didn't actually measure, but I counted my steps; 95 steps away and it still kept a connection. However, once it lost the connection I had to take 10-15 steps to get it to re-connect. Still...not bad!

Before I put it on her collar, several times a day I'd activate it with her nearby so it plays its tune, and I'd give her a treat. Hoping she'd learn to hear the tune and come home for a treat. Well that part worked. When she's in range, I click "find" to play the tune and she runs home for her treat. Or perhaps she's running home because she's freaked out about this music that's chasing her. Either way, success!

The only downfall is that sometimes she's 10 feet away and it will say "out of range". If I stand there long enough it does usually connect, but it's frustrating to wait for it to catch up. Also, the dotted circle that's supposed to tell you if you're getting hot or cold isn't always very accurate. So I find myself walking back and forth quite a bit feeling like I'm being punk'd by my own cat.

All in all, it's surpassed my expectations. I've been able to find her every time. Sometimes it takes a lot longer since it has trouble connecting at times. I'd give it 4.5 stars if I could, but since I can't, I'll give it 5 since I'm using it for something it's not even advertised to do, and it's still doing it quite well.

Update 9/16/16: well I've had the Tile for almost a year now and I still think this thing is pretty wonderful. It has its moments where it just won't connect, sometimes for hours, but that's very rare. For the most part it's been really solid. I wanted to share what just happened a little while ago. It was around 8pm and my cat was nowhere to be seen. Very unusual for her. She never wants to be outside when it's dark. So I grabbed my phone and went searching in her usual spots. Nothing. Finally I see my Tile app shows her as nearby and connects so I can ring her Tile. I could just barely hear it ringing but finally found that the ringing was coming from a neighbor's garage! Our garages are lined up in the alley behind our condos and without the Tile I never would have even thought to look near the garages, and I never would have known which one she was in. There's a stretch of about 50 of them. As soon as I went up to the garage door and called her she meowed her little head off. I was able to ask the owner to open the door so I could get her out. Without the tile I would have been up all night looking for her and worried sick and what if the owner of that garage was not planning to open it for several days?! I get sick even thinking about it. So.. Here I am ordering 2 more tiles for my other cats even though they never go anywhere. I will just feel better if they have them. Tile has a customer for life right here, especially after tonight!

title: Nice little clock with bluetooth at reasonable price

It comes with several docking templates to hold either an Android phone or iPhone on the dock. It only comes with the micro USB cable for Android, not the Apple cable, which is understandable. The docking feature will work if your smart phones have a slim case, not the ugly Otterbox. If you have a tablet, I don't think the dock connection will hold its weight. When in Bluetooth mode, it is actually good enough to take the phone call on it and the speaker is a lot louder than the phone. For music play back, it is similar to any other clock radio, don't expect a lot of bass out of the speaker! I don't understand why many also complained about the unit does not have Apple cable. title: Cheap, trash.  2 units both malfunctioning within 2 months.
text:
Please stop leaving comments for electronics until you've owned it for several months!!!! (People leaving early reviews are seriously tainting ratings with glowing, positive reviews on brand new items they've only just received. This product is just such a product.)

Sony used to make good quality products, of which I've owned many. Those days are gone. I purchased 2 of these units and both of them were experiencing problems within 40 to 60 days of purchase. When you hold these units in your hands, you'll immediately become doubtful of how long they'll last, just as I did. They feel like cheap plastic toys, not appliances built to last. I have Sony DVD players that are 10 years old and still work perfectly, but these Blu-Rays are junk.

Both of these Blu-Ray units are freezing frequently during Netflix streaming and will even totally lock-up, requiring the unit to actually be unplugged and plugged back in before you can resume function. During a lock-up, none of the buttons on the remote, or on the unit itself will do anything when pressed. Power resetting is the only way to fix a lock-up. Lock-ups are now happening 2 to 3 times a day on each unit. The Netflix freezing is definitely caused by these units, as I have a different brand streaming unit to test with, and streaming works perfectly with the test unit. The freezing only happens with the Sony's and it didn't happen at all when they were brand new. (These units have current firmware installed, too, so that's not a problem. My units were also shipped separately so it's extremely unlikely that mishandling during shipping could have caused these units to go defective.) DON'T BUY THESE JUNKERS, YOU'LL REGRET IT.

title: Amazing TV for average Joe like me
text:
Amazing TV for average Joe like me.

Local giant computer store ran out of a sale item, and they sold this tv (65UF8500) at the same sales price ( 1/2 of current price listed here as of June 30, 15 - $1100).

The IPS screen is looking very sharp and clear from any angles (exclude 3Ds, it appears), and color/contrast looks better than its 60inc brother (60UF8500) - 65 inch is way bigger than 60 inch and somehow this makes screen looks much better and sharper.

I tested HEVC codec 4K movies (downloaded to USB 3.0 thumbdrive) and it played very smoothly (except for a couple of them which said "unable to play back" ).

I love having passive 3d. Some people review passive 3D is not good as active crystal glasses 3D. When I compared this TV to my 3D Projector, which uses active 3D glasses, it was easier on my eyes and equally looked great, if not much more clear without ghosting.
Now I don't have to fumble with USB charging and no more "forget to charge glasses" or buying new batteries.

Playing 3D content via USB thumb drive worked fine, but I had to define whether it's SBS or TB despite "AUTO" setting - maybe it's just me doesn't know how to configure....
I have not tested playing 3D via 3D bluray player yet for my kids misplaced the blurays.....

WebOS 2.0 is easy to use interface for USB, Local NAS (DNLA), Youtube. I was not able to test Netflix or Amazon prime for I don't have account with them.

LG Magic remote is fun to use and it controls my LG 3D bluray player over network.

Builtin WIFI has no issue streaming movie from my networked hard drive.

TV is very thin - about 1 inch near the edge and about 2 inch in the middle (compared to my 42 inch 4K computer monitor, it's 1/2 thin), but I think their thinnest model cost $1000 more....

You may want to invest in HDMI cable if you are going to hookup with AV Stereo or Bluray.
I have not connected this TV to my AV stereo or computer. But from past experience with 4K display on my computer and 42 inch 4K monitor, I actually had to buy HDMI 2.0 compatible cable with 10.3gbs bandwidth to play 4K content - regular 1080P HDMI with "Plays HD content with 3D" labeled cables just wan't good enough to handle 4K content without some some artififacts - such as while line/dots, low sync rate under 30hz... Go with higher bandwidith HDMI cables that says HDMI 2.0 or 4K compatible (they are usually $20 and up at local computer store).

This is an awesome TV.

text:
Astonishing disappointment. I paired these with a new Yamaha R-N303BL stereo receiver. I got back into vinyl a few years ago and wanted to use this set-up primarily for records. Was placing them in a room roughly 18x18 with closed walls and a low ceiling. By the specs (wattage of the amp, dynamic range, etc) these should sound incredible with that pairing.

Not even close.

Never in my wildest dreams did I think these would sound this lackluster. Seemed to struggle getting volume out of them. High end was tinny, low end ranged from non-existent to muddy. I was so distraught I pulled out my old pair of Infinity 2000.6s which are beyond beat up and had actually been in a flood a few years ago. Amazingly, they showed better range than these.

Now granted, some of this may come down to this particular amp as the Yamaha has atrocious push button bass and treble adjustment that allows absolutely zero fine tuning. Also, these may do better when using a sub to take some of the work out of the low end on these, but given their size (these things are friggin' MASSIVE for bookshelf speakers), and what they claim for the dynamic range and the room size I have them in, there is no way these should struggle as badly as they are. Perhaps I just got a bad pair.

Last but not least, they're really ugly speakers. Mine were the walnut finish, which I thought would look nice as they were being placed on a walnut cabinet, but the finish looks completely plastic and fake. The fronts then being black plastic make them look both cheap and old fashioned. An attractive speaker is one you want to leave the grilles off of and show the world. These you'll definitely want to leave covered and as out of sight as possible.

title: Great value, and easily adapted to be solar/eclipse binoculars ...
text:
Great value, and easily adapted to be solar/eclipse binoculars for the August 21, 2017 total solar eclipse. For info on how to use 1.5" Bsaader solar filters from Draco Productions ($7.50 + $1.50 S&H), Here are the plans.
Making Solar Filters for Tasco 10x25 Binoculars:
Materials:
2 Kodak 35 mm film canisters
Draco Baader 1.5” binocular filter set ($7.50 + $1.50 S&H)
[...]
Exacto knife (scissors will not work on film canisters)
.5” wide double stick tape
10x25 Tasco binoculars ($13 at WalMart OR Gander Mountain)
If you want to use them with the 10x25 binocular (or the 10x25 monocular from Gander Mountain for $10), you can temporarily remove the rubber shield over the front end as shown below, and the film canister will then fit over the bare metal tube.
Use the knife to cut out a 1” wide hole in the bottom of each
canister as show here. The 1.5” Baader solar filter will be placed in front of this hole to allow sunlight into the binoculars.
Now using ½” wide double stick tape, place strip around the bottom end of the canister. This is the portion of the canister than will fit on the end of the binocular and hold the solar filter.
Use the Exacto knife to cut along the edge of the .5” tape; go all the way around the canister to cut off the end with the hole in it; this part of the canister will exactly cover the metal tube.
Place the canister, bottom down, on the center of the 1.5” Baader filter.
Fold the edges of the filter up to stick them in place with the sticky tape. Keep the center of film flat.
Now place the front rubber shield over the top of the filter and canister to hold and protect the solar filter in place.
You are now ready to slip the filters back on the front of your binoculars for safe solar viewing. Of course, remove the filters to observe anything other than the sun.
Place the solar filters on the front of each side of the binoculars. You are now ready to safely observe the sun.
Any sunspot as large as the Earth will be seen with the 10x binocs on the white disk of the Sun, and you may be able to see brighter patches, called faculae, nearby as well with the 10X binocs. They will be ideal for convenient observing of the solar eclipse visible in the US on August 21, 2017. During totality only, it is safe to observe the Sun directly without Baader filters. The partial eclipse should be observed only with these filters in place!
Should these filters become tarnished by fingerprints, or scratched, do not use and order replacements from Draco. It is suggested that the filters be stored safely in a Ziploc bag when they are not being used for safe solar observing
I recommend these binoculars and filters to everyone; the price is good, and these binoculars perform surprisingly well in a variety of activities, such as bird watching, camping, hiking, and astronomy at night as well. They are light and compact enough to be kept in a pocket or purse, and 10X is about the highest power many people can hold easily without noting shaking of the hands

title: The best designed camera rig in the world. But use caution or you might end up with a broken camera.
text:
The positive:

-There is nothing else on the market that does what this does. It is lightweight and since you have the strap around your shoulder (be sure to tighten this as much as you can, if you dont this will not work very well) to help hold the weight of the camera instead of putting a lot of counterweights on the back like on other rigs.
-Unlike other rigs that needs lots and lots of rails and adjustments to make the camera sit where you like it, here you can easily place the viewfinder of your camera/DSLR right in front of your eye, or have the camera far enough in front of you so your eyes can focus on the LCD screen of the camera. This adjustment only takes a few seconds unlike the rigs that will need you to move things around quite a bit. You can adjust this rig anyway you like. Like me you will probably not understand just how adjustable it is before you try it in real life.

The negative:

While the design of the rig is totally genious the build quality is not. For this kind of money I totally understand that you can't expect everything. There is however one major flaw with it. The plastic it is made of at first seems really solid. It is very thick and it seems very sturdy. The longest extender will make you nervous because it is quite thin. But the other pieces seem solid enough. I have used my rig three times and loved using it. And because the plastic is so thick I really didnt worry too much about its build quality.

That was until this morning.....on my way out to a shoot I just wanted to adjust the rig a bit. Happily the camera was not mounted on it while doing this. When i tightened the screw that goes into the short piece that will raise the camera in height suddenly that whole piece came apart. The reason for this is that the plastic it is made of is very dry/porous. In the bottom of this piece there is a metal wingnut that is just glued/put up into the bottom of the plastic. When you use a bit of force to tighten the screw that goes through this wingnut a few times the plastic will sooner or later come apart from the pressure. The plastic that was holding the wingnut on mine had just colapsed into many small pieces from the force of tightening the screw just a few times. After seeing just how little force the plastic was able to hold I am happy that this happened without the camera on the rig. If this had been made by a quality manufacturer they would have put a bigger piece of metal into the various plastic pieces. This would have been able to withstand the force from both holding the camera and tightening the screws more than a few times. The other pieces that you can put on it have a different design where the wingnuts just put pressure on each side of the plastic. These can break as well but not as easy. So the big design flaw is in the one piece that will raise the camera about an inch. But this piece is fundamental for all uses where you want to put the viewfinder close to you eyes.

This is really sad since there is nothing else in the market today that will do the job as well as this as lightweight and quick. Since there is no other alternatives I will go ahead and buy another one. But this time I will make sure to never tighten that one screw much at all. That way it might hold together a little bit longer. I expect mayby 10-20 times of use if I am lucky. I will actually buy a few more and use them as a disposable thing that you will expect to break every now and then.

Conclusion:
I wish that someone would copy this design and make a more solid version. Still mainly in plastic to keep the weight light. But make sure there is enough metal used around the screws for it to not come apart this quickly. I would be happy to pay ten times the price for a really solid version of this product that you could rely on.

If you consider buying this item you should really try it out but use caution:

-do not trust it to hold your expensive camera. Never ever let go of it. Always keep at least one hand on the camera in case the rig collapses. The rig will carry the cameras weight but keep the one hand ready to tighten the grip on the camera just in case.
-dont expect this to last very long. If you dont need the one piece that heightens the camera I would guess that you can expect it to last much longer.
-dont put a heavy camera on the rig. If you are planning on using the long piece that extends the camera away from you body a DSLR is the max weight I would have tried doing this with. With a camcorder the rig will get very front heavy and the long plastic piece will sooner or later break in two. The rig might however be able to carry a camcorder if you put it close to you body and use its viewfinder. But hold on to it cause it might still break when you least expect it to.

Now you are warned and hopefully you will be able to use this rig without your camera falling to the ground.

text: Check out the frequency specs for this filter. This filter lets frequencies between 470 - 790 MHz through. In the USA the higher limit for UHF is 700 MHz. Do you see the problem? You want all frequencies above 700MHz to be filtered out and this filter starts at 790MHz. AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile all have frequencies in that upper range of this filter. I believe T-Mobil in the summer of 2017 won a 30 MHz chunk range in the 600 MHz area to be used for 4G LTE. Do yourself a favor and get a Channel Master CM3201 LTE line filter or some equivalent because you want to filter out those upper frequencies above 700MHz.

title: Excellent scart cable, no noise
text:
These are excellent scart cables. The connector is actually screwed together unlike most, so it won't come apart or come loose. The outer sheathe is heavy duty rubber insulation. The individual wires inside are heavily insulated, which is why the outer diameter is so thick.

As a bonus the connectors have a cool chrome look, which is nice.

You really can't get quality cables like this at least in the US for this price (or maybe even at all)

Bought several of these to chain various scart switches together for my gaming setup, and they work great. They introduced no noise, and video is very clear.

The only potential cons are that the connectors are heavy since they are metal, and the cable can take up a lot of space/isn't necessarily as flexible as smaller cables, so in some tight spaces or orientations this may not work out for you.

Something worth noting: These cables at first appeared to introduce noise into my duo-rx, but on further testing i concluded it was just making the image slightly sharper, and the noise was caused by a particular socket in one of my scart switches. The noise was always there but became more noticeable with this cable. When switching to a different socket on the switch the problem was gone. So make sure you are using high quality switches (that particular one in my setup is not)

title: DUST FREE !
text: Great ! I got it installed with no bubbles or dust spots. Here are a few tips. First lay the protector on the screen before you take off anything and line it up, then take Scotch tape and tape it on one end to hold it in place. Then lift up the loose end and lay it off of the screen. Now you don't have to worry about lining it up again, the tape will keep it in place. Now clean the screen with just a new microfiber cloth. If you need to use water make sure you only use distilled water because it is pure. Make sure it is dry, then use Scotch tape and use it to take off any dust. I don't mess around and use a lot of tape because it's the only way to get most dust off of the screen. Now peel off the # 1 part of the protector off and slowly place the protector  on while using the the included applicator to remove bubbles. Then remove # 2 and then only use the microfiber cloth to get any remaining bubbles out so you don't scratch the protector. If there are any dust spots left you can use Scotch tape to lift the protector up again to use more tape to remove the dust spot. Keep in mind the dust will most likely be on the protector not the screen, so use it on both. The trick to using tape to lift it up again is to do it on the edge of the protector. I must have put on at least 30 protectors and slowly learned the tricks. Make sure you do it where it is not dusty. I use a Swifter dust cloth to dust the area first then go in a different room and shake any dust off of myself before starting. I hope this helps anyone that is new to this. Good Luck !

title: A costly lesson
text:
I purchased nexstar 5se telescope and had it delivered on 3.Sept.2015 (India). I have had trouble with it from day 1. The following are the issues.

1. Battery life is low: The battery power does not last more than 10 to 15 minutes. I have wasted 4 sets of batteries. I had read about this issue when I was reading reviews, but not everyone had this issue.
Solution: I was told to use high amperage batteries by the vendor. (Looks like I need to have a separate budgeting every month just to buy batteries) OR buy a celestron powertank.

2. Poor response from motors: The remote works fine when I change the directions of the telescope without any problems. As soon as I try to use skyalign, the motor response become extremely slow. The issue starts when I try to align the 2nd object and continues into 3rd object. I tried using celestron powertank and had the same issue.

3. Skyalign does not work: I have tried using skyalign technology; 8 out of 9 times, it has failed to align. The one time it aligned, the telescope was pointing everything in the wrong direction.

4. Trembling tripod: The tripod trembles under slightest of wind. There is lot of shaking when I try to focus the object on the OTA.

5. Star finderscope has shortcomings: The object located at the center of Finderscope does not aligh with OTA. There is loose connection in the switch.

6. I am really surprised there is no power adapter given along with the product. Looks like the battery issue is a known problem with your product. Please include atleast in future packages as it provides backup to your customers.

I am very unhappy with the overall product with the exception of the optics. It has been 12 days and I have not had a single day I was able to enjoy the telescope. I had read very bad support reviews for Celestron. My only hope now is that, the product has 2 year warranty and expect it to make it work some time in the future.

A costly bitter lesson.

Anyway, this year the Tom finally started dying out on me - it wouldn't update correctly, it'd delete itself randomly... I had driven from Iowa to Kansas when this happened, so I decided that I needed to replace my model.

The top-of-the-line GPS devices are very affordable now because most people just use the built-in Google Map navigation app on their phones - GPS companies know this, which is why even the top models are not that expensive now (keep in mind, my Tom cost $100 for just a base-line model - the same price now will get you one of their best rated models instead).

My Garmin is easy to use, easy to update, came with everything that I needed (USB cord, car charger, and car mount for the GPS). I chose this also because of the free lifetime maps update. I highly recommend... it might cost you now, but it'll be worth it in the long run - as I've stated, I had a refurbished, base-line TomTome ONE series for over six years before replacing for a more modern and advance one - so I imagine I'd get at least ten years out of this one.

title: Great picture, easy to use guide, good price, flexible expansion capability.
text:
I was pretty frustrated with this Tabo Dual Lite at first. At first I tried connecting via wi-fi, and not only was it difficult to set up, but the connection was never reliable. On wi-fi, the Tablo would disconnect at least once a day, and never reconnect. My Google wifi mesh gives a very strong signal, so I don’t think it’s my Wi-Fi. After struggling with it for a few days, I gave up on wi-fi and plugged it in to one of the google mesh access points. That resolved all of the connectivity issues. Connecting to the Tablo has been rock solid ever since.

The Tablo is connected to an antenna in my attic. It pulls in at least 30 stations in my area, and there are never any glitches in the picture. In my area, most major stations are 720p, and I have the Tablo set at its highest bandwidth setting, 10 Mbps. On a 55 inch screen, the picture is perfect. On my theater projector, It’s not perfectly sharp, but very good nevertheless.

I added a 1TB USB3 drive for ~$50 for hundreds of hours of DVR capacity.

The guide works very well; selecting a station is simple and easy, much like a cable box, at least on an Apple TV. I’m still on the 30 day trial for the guide subscription, but I’ll probably spring for the lifetime subscription deal if the Tablo continues to work as well as it has been after 30 days.

Here are some observations about the Tablo:

* It takes a long time for the Tablo to download the guide data the first time. The Tablo upgraded its firmware and rebooted while the guide data was downloading the first time, and after that the guide was not usable, so I had to go into settings and force it to refresh the guide data.

* If you find that the Tablo freezes or you can’t find it on the network after setting it up, try connecting it via an ethernet cable to your router. It seems to be a lot happier that way.

* The Tablo gets hot to the touch and has no fan. It makes me wonder how long it will last. I keep it in a room with plenty of ventilation and no other heat sources. Time will tell if the excessive heat is a problem.

* If you spring for the guide subscription, I believe it will also let you watch the Tablo while traveling. I haven’t tried this, but it might be useful when traveling overseas, where most streaming services are blocked.

* if you’re a cord cutter, like me, then this pairs up very well with Philo TV. The only thing I’ll be missing is ESPN, FX, and USA. I can live without them.

* On an Apple TV it's possible to switch to other stations without leaving the current station. Just swipe down on the remote. It will list other stations you can watch. It's not a full guide, but it's useful.

title: My first and favorite Camera~
text:
This Camera has been with me for the almost two years it's been out.

I've aimed to take my photography seriously and professionally and let me just say - Jumping in head first instead of taking baby steps with a t3i series camera seemed to do the trick. I've studied, I've worked hard and I've gotten better and better at my photography. This camera has easily became more of a life-long soul partner with the experiences of everything I've learned with it. Between learning the white balance, mainly using manual (Aperture control or Bulb in a few other cases.) and learning how to quickly get in and out of focus, I've really gotten to experience what it is to be a competent photographer and don't have a thing to complain about when using my 70D.

Infact the only issue I have now is that I wish Canon would send me more of those expensive lens for free so I can get a chance to experience faster shutter speeds, but alas this is not a perfect world.

I've gotten a chance to use both photo and video side of things and both work exceedingly well without need for editing. Using lightroom or final cut for the photos/videos only make the photos turn out exceptionally amazing from what they already are. The flow of being able to switch my white balance, aperture, iso and etc. easily from the quick view makes it an enjoyable experience and having a favorite menu list only makes accessing more extensive stuff smoother when I'm in the middle of serious shoots. It gets even better knowing that I can easily make composite photos or take some unedited photos and just toss them on my phone easily due to the cellphone app and wireless feature of the camera.

This thing is a beast and adding better lens/flashes to said beast only makes it unleash a grizzlier beast. I may be rambling, but trust and believe that this camera is worth the money and that the lens is a decent starter lens to go with. I've read before that some had issues with their AF features on first purchases, but I was fortunate enough to not experience that issue, so for someone who got a fully capable working 70D - my say is to go ahead and get it unless you're wealthy enough to get yourself a 5DS R.

title: Too Many Problems
text:
I was very excited to use this printer for an extended trip abroad. The first picture that came out of the printer was great! After that, the quality has gone consistently downhill. The photos come out very dark, with a slight pink cast to them. If I use the editor to brighten the photos first, they print out very desaturated, almost black and white. This problem persists despite updating the firmware, factory resetting the printer, and repeatedly using the blue ZINK Smartsheet that came with the pack of genuine HP paper. After reading that the Polaroid ZINK paper works better provided it is used with the HP blue card, I tried that, but all of the photos had a very pink cast to them. HP has made the blue card "pack specific", presumably to discourage the use of comparable but less costly papers. In searching through the HP help forums, I have read (from HP) that the printer needs to cool down between prints in order for the prints to come out correctly. My printer stays warm for a long, long time, which would possibly explain why the prints are so dark, except that the first one when it's completely cool is dark as well. In addition, the battery charge does not last very long at all. I can only print 3-5 photos on one charge. All things considered, the photo paper for this machine is too costly for the quality it now produces. If it would produce photos of the quality of that very first one that came out, I'd be completely satisfied. What I'm getting out of it now is just unacceptable.

EDIT to add: I forgot a few things. I have to go through my photos on the app and select the one I want to print, then turn on the Sprocket and print it, because the printer will time out in the time it takes me to scroll through the photos. Also, the updates take a really long time to download and heat up my phone, taking the battery down about 50% in the span of about 15 minutes. I have a phone with an extended life battery, so this is pretty ridiculous. In the "help" section, it does say to plug in the phone to ensure that it stays on long enough to finish the update, so it seems to be a known issue.

title: GREAT notepad/doodle board!  Keeps my autistic 4 year old busy at church
text:
My 4 year old son with autism has never had any interest in coloring with crayons and he likes using pens on paper but gets really aggressive and doesn't stay on the paper. There are doodling apps for iPad but if he has an iPad in his hands (which he adores) he's going to be watching YouTube kids, not drawing with his finger.

I was hoping that this device would entice him to practice his pencil holding skills and dexterity, save us going through lots of paper and pens and getting unwanted ink everywhere, and hopefully entertain him at church for a short time, haha!

What I like about it is how thin and light it is! I can easily throw this in any bag and not even notice it's there. The color of the marks that appear is vivid green and very appealing. The flat pencil like stylus that comes with the board is easy to hold and manipulate for adults or children. I love that the pencil clips into place at the base of the board so you don't have to worry about it floating loose in a bag or getting lost but you still have the freedom to write uninhibited unlike with those magnetic doodle boards where the stylus is attached by a string.

My son likes that it appears somewhat like an iPad and he can push the "home button" to erase and start over as often as he wants.

A few things to note:
- Yes it is battery operated (1 3V comes pre installed)
- No it doesn't have any sort of internal storage, connect to computers or save pictures or doodles
- You can scan and save/share your images with a free app on your phone or tablet
- It has magnets on the back enabling you to stick it easily to a fridge to jot down notes or display artwork or whatever. It sticks firmly enough not to be dislodged if the fridge door slams shut. That's a great feature
- The screen does respond with some degree of sensitivity to the amount of pressure you push down with (see pic)
- There is absolutely no delay in either the writing or the erasing. It is instantaneous
- Be aware that if you write along the very edges of the screen, the lines will blur and even change color in spots (see pic)

All in all this thing is very well made, compact and cool. It does what it advertises to do and does it well. I would definitely recommend!

PS: I was NOT given this item free or at a discount in exchange for a review! I paid full price for it and am writing this review just because I want to help other people who are paying full price for stuff too! :D

title: Love this thing! Solved my placement problem
text:
I live in a house that's 110 years old. That means, lots of plaster, metal lathe, etc. Those walls seriously impact the performance of most wifi units. It also means that I don't always have power outlets where I'd want them. I kept thinking about how I'd be able to place my access point where I'd wanted to do so, without having to run new power to an odd location. Because this unit UAP-AC-LR came with the the POE power injector I was able to string some new Cat 6 cable high up on a wall in the center of my house and voila, wifi in my entire house. The signal has to go through 2 to 3 walls in several areas of the house and go about 25 to 30 feet in any direction. I get great coverage everywhere, except for the basement. I have another AP there to handle that. I have 100 - 130 Mbps wired and I get about 65 Mbps on my phone within 5 feet of this thing and typically about 40 Mbps when at the edges of the house. Worst performance is behind a TV on the wall (where I have a Chromecast) where the speed is only like 10 - 20 Mbps. But this is far and away better overall performance than my poorly placed wired AP / router. I couldn't place my router/AP where I wanted because of the power location.

I had the unit, unpacked it, ran some new cable (as a test) and had it configured and working within an hour, and had the cable run properly and all hung up on my wall within 2 hours.

I found that the initial configuration (which had a simple wizard) was really really easy. But, after I found out it worked like I wanted, I wanted to rename it and do a few other things, and the configuration tool (which you have to download) was not particularly straightforward. Some of the options are not labeled intuitively. But, even given that frustration, it still was only 2 hours start to finish.

I even had a power outage 1 day after install and it restarted and worked again without any work from me, which I clearly like. It's been running flawlessly for a week now. Can't be happier.

title: MASSIVE improvement over my old radio headphone ear protection
text:
I had been mowing the grass and working in my shop while wearing 3M's 'WorkTunes' version of these for the past 4 years until last week when they somehow managed to fall off the hook I usually hang them from and found their way under my brother's truck tire. After almost buying a new set of the same kind I instead decided to pay a little more and give this Stanley Sync RST-63012 a try instead and I'm so glad I did. I now feel a bit guilty for the grief I gave my brother for breaking my old ones because I now realize he did me a huge favor. Had I known how much better these are, and conversely how terrible those Worktunes were, I would have ran the old set over myself a long time ago. :P

Some reasons why these are so much better:
- I now have at least 12 stations come in loud and clear regardless of where I am on my property, inside or out. The old ones only received 3-4 and even then the reception was iffy. A simple turn of my head or direction on the mower would often result in static.
- These block out more noise. These are rated "NRR 25 dB" and the Worktunes are rated 'NRR 24 dB', but the difference seems noticeably better than those numbers suggest.
- The volume adjusts louder - Not ear-blasting loud but at least now I can actually hear the radio over the mower or table saw. I can even listen to news on NPR and clearly understand all of what's being said. That was never an option with the Worktunes even in the rare instance when I did manage to get in a position where the channel would come in moderately static-free.

I did notice a few cons though:
- The instruction manual came hidden between the two pieces of cardboard in the package backing. It would be very easy to miss it there.
- The method of operation is not at all intuitive. You likely will need to read the instructions to know how to turn it off/on, switch between am/fm and preset any of the stations into memory
- The manual print is very small.

If you don't have the manual, here's what you need to know:
- The batteries go in easy enough and do have small symbols that should make it fairly straightforward. Push in where it says "Push" and the cover slides up and off. The included AA batteries go in with the positive (+) up on the left and the neg (-) up on the right.

- The opposite ear muff has all the controls:
-- The bottom has a volume knob and a 3.5mm jack for attaching a phone or mp3 player or the like.
-- There are four buttons on the side in a diamond pattern with a display above them.
--- The bottom button has a power symbol on it. Press and hold it for ~two secs or so to turn it on or off, and while it is on press this same button quickly to switch between AM and FM.
--- The left and right buttons have '<' '>' symbols on them respectively and are used for tuning stations. Press and hold either for ~2 secs to auto-tune to the next available station that comes in clearly or press and release quickly to manually tune one step at a time through the frequency band.
--- The top button has an 'M' on it for 'Memory'. While the headphones are on and tuned to a station that you want to save as a preset, press and hold the top (M) button for ~2 secs until the display flashes, then quickly while it is still flashing use the '<' and '>' buttons to select the preset number (0-9) you wish to save the station as, and lastly press the top (M) button again to save it as the preset number you selected. Once you have more than one saved, press and quickly release the top (M) button to switch between your preset stations.

title: Great quality and a great price
text:
This is a great quality product for way less money than some others. I put this on my new iPad Pro 9.7 because I'm a big believer in screen protectors and I've always preferred the glass ones to the rubbery ones.

Installation went better than expected and I liked that the print on the instruction booklet was in print large enough to read easily. They key to a good install is making sure the screen is super clean. But just in case you get a bit of dust or pet hair under it, there are some sticky tapes in the package to remove them. All you have to do is lift the glass and press the tape on the spot to remove it. Once you have it all clean, press it down and use the included squeegee to get it properly attached. I usually have to stick these things 2 or 3 times to get them right, but not with this one. It went right on straight on the first try.

I was a bit concerned about whether the Apple pencil would work the same as without the screen protector. But there was no problem with that. So for anyone wondering if you can use the Apple pencil with a glass screen protector, the answer is, yes.

Another big advantage for me was seeing that dust and pet hair doesn't stick to the glass as badly as it did without the protector.

The only thing that bothered me a little is that it adds some gloss to the display. It's not that bad, but maybe I just noticed it because the anti-glare on the new iPad Pro is seriously amazing. Still, I think the trade off is worth it for the added protection and not having to worry if the Apple pencil will scratch the display. You hardly notice that it's there (as you can see in the photo) and invisible protection is the whole reason you use these.

Overall, I'm very satisfied and even happier that it didn't cost $49 like some other brands. I highly recommend this screen protector.

title: I've owned every version of the Orochi because I like the wired/BT option
text:
I'll state up front, I did not purchase this mouse through Amazon, but directly from Razer as a pre-order.

I've owned every version of the Orochi because I like the wired/BT option, portability and configuration it offers compared to other options on the market. The latest version builds on the previous two with a slightly smoother finish, chroma lighting option for the scroll wheel (nice option if you happen to not be a big fan of Razer's obsession with green - sorry Razer), and some changes to the form with the addition of a textured grip surface to the side coves and slightly enhanced ridges on the top buttons that help guide finger placement. Overall, the minor changes are welcome and only further perfect the virtually flawless form factor.

The Orochi always provided a very satisfying experience with precise operation, virtually unlimited adjustment options through the Synapse software, and unbelievably solid button and scroll wheel action, but I have to mention a persistent problem I experienced with the first two iterations when operating in wired mode. I always had to plug and unplug the mouse several times before the laptop would recognize it. In wireless/BT mode it always "fired right up," but despite multiple uninstall/re-installs of the driver/Synapse program on all of my computers, it never quite worked right when using the USB connection. It was extremely annoying (especially when trying to do Synapse updates), but I put up with it because once it was finally recognized, it was such a great mouse. I'm happy to report as soon as I plugged in this newest version into my laptop, it was recognized immediately and operated flawlessly -- FINALLY!!!

I think Razer is going to have a hard time making this mouse any better than it already is.

title: 60 Mile Omni Circular - great little antenna....should have done this long ago.
text:
Compact, unobtrusive, easy to install and it works. No more huge "spider beast" antenna.
I purchased the 60 mile Omni Circular antenna and put it on the east corner of the top of my chimney, about 30 feet up, and it pulls in almost 100 stations. Most don't interest me, but the ones that do come from nearly 50 miles away and are clear and pixelation free. I also use the amplifier that came with the antenna.
According to DTV reception maps on the FCC website, the stations come from the north (~50mi), east(~35mi) and south(~20mi) and the omni-directional lets me change channels without messing with the antenna. There are hills and trees but no mountains between the stations and my home, and I'm in a suburban setting. So far the weather has been good so I can't speak to foul weather performance, but it has been excellent for the stations I watch (mostly the major networks and everything included with a basic cable subscription).
Combining this with the Mediasonic HDTV converter box and a USB hard drive is a total OTA PVR/media player system and makes a basic cable subscription redundant and unnecessary (and I can zip thru the commercials on playback)
Since the antenna is very compact and weatherproof; I just purchased another one to put on a camper conversion as an experiment to see if it can provide reception when I'm in the boonies. We'll see....
Feb 2016 Update: the antenna on the townhouse has been working just fine, no degradation during rainstorms (what little we have) and no other issues.
I installed one of these on my camper conversion and it is also working great. Mounted it on a pivoting mast that puts it down on the roof when driving, but can raise it 40 inches when settled into a campsite. Reception is good when the antenna is in the down position (4" above the roof) but even better when the mast is up and the antenna is 12 feet high. With the Omni-directional antenna I just pivot the mast up and don't worry about where to point it or what channel I'm watching. It's not satellite, so there are places with no reception, but no monthly fee either and it doesn't eat battery power.

title: The Aluminum BeFree with Carbon Fiber Legs! BeFree To A Price Point!
text:
[[VIDEOID:bfb47c7e6566c86feec90d5b6d95d0]] I bought the Manfrotto BeFree Carbon Fiber Tripod to use with my Nikon D5100 for outdoor and indoor video and photography. It is a nice tripod and a decent deal if you can get it on sale for less than its list price. It is not a no-compromises tripod and typical with things built to a price point, it has its pros and cons.

Its good for hiking and travel but I wouldn't use it for serious work. Some competitors:
The MeFoto Backpacker - [[ASIN:B00BETIULM MeFOTO C1350Q1T Carbon Fiber Roadtrip Travel Tripod Kit (Titanium)]]
Amazon Carbon Fiber - [[ASIN:B00DHPCSA0 AmazonBasics 52-Inch Carbon Fiber Travel Tripod with Bag]]
3-legged Thing - [[ASIN:B00XCWB8Q8 3 Legged Thing EVO3 Punks Rick Carbon Fiber Tripod and Mohawk Ball Head]]

Pros:
Light and compact - The BeFree only weights 2.4lbs. It folds up really small, is incredibly light, and I can take it on long hikes without it weighing me down.

The tripod is solid. It does have some wobble at full extension is stable at minimum extension. The heads locks down tight and the center column doesn't wobble. The fact that the legs are carbon fiber leads me to my next point ...

Carbon Fiber - The legs are made of carbon fiber. Carbon fiber naturally dampens vibrations and ensures and shaking is quickly stopped.

Spare parts are easily available - Unlike cheaper tripods, this tripod is considered to be premium and, including aluminum ones, 100s of thousands have been sold. This means that parts are easily available. You can easily buy parts directly from Manfrotto or salvage them from older tripods.

Cons:
The bag is flimsy. The zipper feels cheap and I can see the bag deforming where the handle connects to it just after a few trips.

Wobbly when fully extended - Even though it is carbon fiber. it doesn't have spiked feet or a hook to hang a bag off for stability. It will wobble even in light wind and shooting a timelapse in any kind of wind is futile.

Compact but not as compact as it could be - It is not usable as a tabletop tripod because the legs splay out even at minimum expansion. I could flip over the camera to be closer to the action but the video would be flipped and the amount of space the tripod takes is still sizable which limits how close it can get to the action.

Only the legs are carbon fiber - The rest of the tripod is aluminum - the center column, the head, the base plate, and the leg connectors are all metal. It should be called the BeFree with carbon fiber legs!

Base plate doesn't have screw slot - The base plate doesn't have a coin slot to unscrew it. It just has a somewhat flimsy handle that I feel will break off after some use.

The baseplate could have been made more stable. My camera doesn't sit flat with the baseplate attached. It tilts over and rests on its lens. I hesitate to remove the baseplate every time I take my camera off the table because like I mentioned above, I feel the screw handle will break off after some use.

Along similar lines, the baseplate has some hard edges. I hesitate to put it table surfaces to avoid scratches. Rubberizing the base of the baseplate would have made sense but again it seems like there was a price point they wanted to hit.

title: Find your keys!  Find your phone!! Tile!!!  (Then Buy a New One!!!!)
text:
Update 3/23/16 - Earlier this month, I tried to check my Tile and the battery was dead. I hadn't checked in a while, so I can't say for sure how long it lasted, but at best, I got 7 months out of it. It's still a very cool gadget, but without a rechargeable or replaceable battery, I'm not sure I can justify buying another 1-2 every year.

-----

The new Tile is great. Once you pair it with your phone, you can ring your phone by pressing the little square, or ring the Tile using your phone app. On top of that, you can call up a map to show the last place your Tile was recorded as being, and on top of THAT, if your Tile finds someone else's app, it can report its location. Very cool - stick this on your keyring, in your backpack, or in anything else you think you might lose.

One limitation - since it only connects as needed, your Tile can't function as a "trusted device" to keep newer Android phones unlocked. It does everything it was designed to do, and does it well, but not that. :)

Update 9/04/15: I tried this under battle conditions this week and it worked great. As I was rushing to get out of the house and to work, I realized I couldn't find my keys. I started the Tile app on my Moto X phone, and a map came up showing that the keys were in my house. I pressed the button in the app to ring the Tile on my keychain, and heard a ringing from behind a shelf in our entry room. Sure enough, there were my keys!

title: DO NOT REFORMAT - SUBJECT TO GRIDLOCK
text:
These may work fine for run of the mill laptop work, but they are a piece of junk for any other use.
I purchased a ten pack to use as linux boot drives for work. That means the first thing to happen to them is a wipe of all partitions and a reformat.

(This is not an uncommon use of these things - just as you might have wanted to use it to boot linux on your desktop, or as a recovery disk for a Mac etc).

Every drive I tried instantly 'gridlocked'. It went read-only via a hardware fault which can not be cleared. This is, surprisingly, a known problem with Sandisk USB drives ... it's just the first time I've ever run across it - and I have flashed hundreds of USB drives, from multiple vendors, over the last 5 years. They are consumables: I don't buy the most expensive because I expect to wear them out and bin them in a few months.

But I'm not even getting a single use from them.

Don't waste your time and money unless they are purely for Windows use and nothing critical.

title: Good component. See notes on pin order.
text:
A well-built board. Very sturdy. The 10 input connections are (left to right, with the input connectors along the bottom)
==> 1 - 8, Switching connection; apply + voltage to close (turn on) the load
==> 9, ground
==> 10, power. +3 - 5v required to turn on any circuit. Removing power will open (turn off) all circuits, even if power is applied to 1 - 8.

The spec sheet suggests +3 - +5 volts as the input (switching) power on pins 1-8 and on pin 10. I tested the input up to 13.5v and found no problems with overheating of the components in the switching circuits.

Note that the load is only switched in one direction. If you reverse the + and - on the load connection, current will flow even with no voltage applied to the input circuit.

title: Excellent case for Fire HD10
text:
I didn't want to spend money on the Amazon cover, so I decided to buy this. I don't regret my purchase at all.

**Pros**

* Snap On Case: I heavily prefer snap on cases to ones with a pouch that you slip the tablet into. The latter looks bulky and unattractive to me. This case snaps onto the back of the tablet. This means no case fabric on the bezels and I get nice glass.

* Sleep on Close: Magnets embedded in the cover makes the tablet go into sleep mode every time I close it. When I open up the cover, the tablet wakes up. Very handy feature and saves on battery life by not leaving the display on if the cover is closed.

* Landscape kickstand: The cover folds back onto itself and becomes a stand for the tablet in landscape. This lets you watch your movies hands-free. Unlike the Amazon cover, this one doesn't give you a stand in portrait mode but I personally never need my tablet standing in that orientation anyways.

* Fit: Everything fits perfectly. The ports are all exposed, speaker holes are exposed, and the fit of the case itself is tight. Simple snap-in and it holds. There's no play between the tablet and case at all unlike slip-in cases I've tried in the past.

Overall I'd highly recommend buying. At the time of my purchase this was the cheapest HD10 case available and I'm extremely happy with this buy.

title: Fast speeds, but micro insertion feels terrible (scraping/crunching sound) and can't read both card slots at same time.
text:
2nd attempt at getting this review approved, don't know what I did wrong before but I have attempted an edit.

Headline says most of it.

---> Notes: Well there was a rant here about a requested change to the advertising of the product features and I had a picture of the packaging but apparently those are no-no's for Amazon reviews these days so since I am only allowed to review the product, here's me stating a fact about it: THIS READER ONLY READS ONE CARD AT A TIME.

DECISION:
Since I've already torn the packaging to open it, and it was such a dirt cheap add-on item I will not be returning it but I will be stashing this as a backup reader in my camera bag instead of using it as my primary card reader. I will be buying a [insert different product here] for about $2 more, like I should have done in the first place, because it can read both card slots simultaneously and I am a fan of [insert different brand here]. Better?

Gripes:
- The micro sd slot sounds terrible when inserting card, like it's full of sand and metal shavings. Still works, but sketches me out and makes me think it's scratching the contacts. Would much prefer a smooth spring-loaded interface like how most cameras and phones have.
- Missing double card reading functionality makes this dead in the water as my primary reader. If you already have a card inserted and you stick a 2nd in, NEITHER shows up, so that's somehow worse than only reading 1 at a time. I was intending to use this to read my 2 dash cam cards at the same time to watch the front and rear footage simultaneously, but obviously that isn't happening.

Good:
- For $6 and some change it works and is USB-3.0-fast (~100 MB/s copy speeds) with one card at a time.
- I like that it has a cap but based on the history of USB devices with removable caps it is very likely to get lost.

Meh:
- It's a little narrower than some similar ones, which I like, but it's still too wide to be used in a side-by-side port on a laptop or USB hub so it's kind of a moot point.
- Cards stick out the left side of the reader with the label facing up, which may interfere more or less with other things you have plugged in depending on your hardware, so check before you buy.
